Outbuilding and barn destroyed. Several large branches broken along the path. Windows blown out of south facing porch.

A tornado developed in open fields near the intersection of 625 Avenue and 725 Road, and moved quickly east. The tornado damaged many trees, flipped pivots, and destroyed at least two large farm sheds. The damage along the track was somewhat sporadic at times, and this concentrated area of tornado damage was embedded within a much broader area of 60 to 80 mph winds in the downdraft regions of the parent thunderstorm. The peak width of the tornado was determined where it traveled through a long line of trees and gave evidence to the most intense focused zone of winds being approximately 200 yards wide.

A tornado developed just south of Highway 136 and west of 636 Avenue, and moved east northeast to the area near Highway 136 and just east of 637 Avenue. This tornado caused sporadic tree damage and uprooting, and impacted two farms. At one farm, a large trailer was rolled approximately 50 yards and debris distributed downstream across a field. Several trees were snapped or uprooted and landed on a home. Another farm had a large shed destroyed with the debris field extending more than a half mile downstream. This tornado was embedded in a broad area of straight line downburst winds estimated at up to 95 mph, especially near and just south of the tornado track.
QLCS tornado resulted in damage to several power poles and large tree limbs. One two-story home had uplift on roof material.
Brief tornado in an open field reported by public. No known damage. Location is an approximation based on video evidence.

Video from broadcast media showed a small, rain-wrapped tornado moving generally eastward just south of Road 733A and Highway 75. Damage consisted of a small cluster of large downed tree branches, with estimated maximum winds of 80 mph.

NWS Damage Survey team confirmed a tornado occured Monday evening, 5/18/2026, beginning at 9:47 PM CDT in southwestern Ray County Missouri. This tornado caused primarily tree damage along its path, but did impact two properties, one north of Fishing River, shortly after the tornado developed. EF1 Damage to two power poles, one out building was noted, along with the roll over of an empty livestock trailer. The tornado resulted in widespread EF1 tree damage near Reynolds Road and W 108th Street. The tornado continued east-northeast, crossing highway 10 south of Elkhorn before causing tree damage north of Swanwick before crossing highway 13. The tornado ended near the intersection of Frazier Road and Millville Road at 10:06 PM CDT.
Old barn lost 30-40% of roof and wall, small barn completely destroyed with debris carried about 1/4 mile ENE.

At approximately 4:55 PM, a tornado developed near the Nebraska/Kansas border just west of 639 Boulevard, damaging some trees. It continued northeast, crossing 639 Boulevard and producing significant damage to the roof of a large metal outbuilding. The tornado then crossed US Highway 75 just northwest of the intersection with 641 Avenue, causing further tree damage and impacting a second metal outbuilding in the area. Additional tree damage occurred near Rock Creek and 642 Avenue, where the tornado came to an end.

A tornado developed at approximately 5:07 PM near the intersection of 646 Avenue and 708 Road, about 1 mile northeast of Salem. Intermittent damage to trees and farm outbuildings was noted between 646 and 647 Avenues. The tornado continued northeast, damaging more trees and breaking power poles along 650 Avenue. Additional damage to trees and farm outbuildings was noted near the intersection of 651 Avenue and 710 Road. The tornado then crossed US Highway 73 and lifted the roof off another farm outbuilding east of 652 Avenue before dissipating shortly thereafter.
Damage along path consistent of weak tornado. SRV Rotational couplet evident at this time. Photo evidence of tornado provided by Ringgold County Emergency Management.

Storm chaser video showed a brief tornado that began just south of State Highway 8, approximately 4.5 miles south-southeast of Diller. It continued northeast, crossing the highway before quickly dissipating. No damage was noted.
Brief tornado in an open field reported by public. No known damage. Location is an approximation based on video evidence.

A combination of radar and Sentinel-2 satellite data concluded an EF0 tornado occurred about 1.5 miles east of Junction Ferry. Satellite data depicted intermittent patches of tree damage in a confined path from County Road P-235 to just east of State Highway 106. Most of the path width ranged from 75 to 125 yards, but at its widest point, the tornado's damage path was measured to be 150 yards in width. The damage path length was 3.54 miles.

A combination of ground surveys, radar data, and Sentinel-2 satellite data concluded an EF0 tornado briefly occurred approximately 2 miles south of White Church. A short 0.6-mile confined path of trees were damaged just east of State Route 17.

A landspout tornado was observed at 3:17 PM EDT near the intersection U.S. Hwy 41/S Cleveland Ave and Gorham Ave, where a citizen submitted video of a rotating cloud base and funnel near the Wawa and Culvers, and later confirmed that they witnessed a ground circulation with surface and lofted dust and small debris. No significant damage was reported, and no other reports, pictures or videos have been received indicating that the track extended beyond that location.

A NWS Damage Survey team confirmed an EF-0 tornado occurred 
Monday evening, 5/18/2026 in and near the city of Fillmore, MO. 
The tornado started at 8:11 PM CDT, southwest of the city of 
Fillmore. The tornado caused EF-0 tree damage southwest of 
Fillmore, and then caused EF-0 damage to several residences and 
outbuildings within the city of Fillmore. The tornado continued to
the northeast of Fillmore, causing more EF-0 tree damage and 
eventually lifting at 8:16 PM CDT 4 miles east northeast of 
Fillmore, near the intersection of County Road 40 and County Road 
55.

A landspout tornado formed over Cape Coral just north of the Sovereign Canal around 3:35 PM EDT in association with a separate segment of the cluster of thunderstorms, with evidence of the circulation visible in video taken by residents along SW 4th Ave and SW 5th Ave. Footage from SW 4th Ave showed a pickup truck in the driveway of a home being displaced a number of feet as the circulation passed by the location, and footage from the SW 5th Ave location showed the funnel of the landspout and the surface circulation behind a home over the Niagara Canal. Additional footage of the circulation was taken approximately one-quarter mile to the northwest near the Seabell Canal, where footage from a home on the southern edge of the canal along SW 26th Ter showed the circulation blowing lawn chairs around and lofting additional unidentified debris, while also knocking over and blowing around vinyl fencing in the backyard of a home on the opposite/northern side of the canal along SW 26th St. A few additional reports and photos from the vicinity also indicated fence and some roof damage as the circulation neared the intersection of Skyline Blvd and Veterans Pkwy before before it is estimated to have dissipated around 3:38 PM EDT, as no other reports, pictures or videos have been confirmed to indicate that the track extended further.

A landspout tornado likely associated with the circulation responsible for a previous landspout is estimated to have formed around 3:25 PM EDT approximately 1.75 miles to the northwest of the previous landspout, where damage was first noted along Reynard Ave in the Tanglewood area where a large tree had numerous medium to large branches snapped. Branches and limbs were snapped at multiple locations across Cumberland and Woodwind Courts, and a home near Tanglewood Pkwy had a large tree uprooted in its yard. Additional footage was submitted from the Tanglewood vicinity depicting lawn furniture and yard decor scattered about, along with fencing and roof damage, and a video taken by a resident along Westminster Dr at 3:28 PM EDT showed airborne debris along with indications of the ground circulation as the landspout neared the McGregor Gardens area and Argyle Dr and McGregor Blvd. The circulation continued northwest across the Georgetown area just south of Colonial Blvd and began crossing the Caloosahatchee River just to the west-southwest of McGregor Colonial Memorial Park, and to the south of the Midpoint Bridge around 3:30 PM EDT. Videos taken by the public showed surface spray associated with the circulation as it approached and crossed the Midpoint Bridge west of McGregor Colonial Memorial Park and continued northwest toward the central section of the river north of the bridge, where it is estimated to have dissipated sometime around 3:31 PM EDT before reaching the western shore of the river.

This weak tornado tracked north northeastward roughly along Midway Road from north of Oakley Palestine Road to Thigpen Road, then lifted near Seven Springs Road. Along the path, several large tree limbs were downed. A tornadic debris signature was observed on radar.
Virtual survey with information from emergency management. 8 power poles broke and splintered. Video confirmed. 82 mph wind gusts recorded at Estherville Airport.

The tornado touched down just north of Interstate 20/59 nearly 2 miles east of exit 89 in a largely open field with a few trees here and there, one of which was uprooted.  Numerous video recordings on social media showed a lowering cloudbase and nebulous funnel cloud crossing the interstate, with what looked like a very narrow drill bit tornado finally touching down.  From there, the tornado moved north, crossing Union Road, where minor damage occurred to a double wide manufactured home and the first hint of a debris signature appeared.  The tornado then traversed inaccessible forests and fields and intensified before reaching K and R Road, where several hardwood and softwood trees were snapped or uprooted.  Only minor damage occurred to any homes on the street.  The tornado then turned more northeasterly, crossed Bama Rock Garden Road—where a carport was tossed and a home sustained other minor damage—and crossed Charles Brook Rd, snapping and uprooting several trees. The tornado dissipated over inaccessible forest somewhere beyond Charles Brook Rd.

A brief tornado occurred in the Exmoor community along County Road 6, between County Road 7 and Lewis Road. The tornado began along the back tree line of a property then moved northeast where it shifted a camper northward a few feet off of its cinder block supports. A manufactured home suffered damage to its porch and awning. Some trees were snapped and uprooted as the tornado crossed County Road 6 before dissipating as it downed trees across the road.

A tornado touched down in New Tazewell on Friday evening. The tornado first touched down along Coffee Road where several hardwood trees were damaged and one home had minor siding damage. The tornado intensified as it approached downtown. Here several building sustained significant damage with several having roof damage. Duncan lumber had multiple building damaged with one sustained major roof uplift and subsequent wall collapse. Other businesses in this area also sustained minor damage. Here the tornado was at it widest point of approximately 75 yards. Several power poled were snapped in this area as well. The tornado then wound down quickly with only very minor roof damage noted along Highway 33 and 5th avenue. Although notable debris was found further downstream of this location no additional damage was identified.

The tornado touched down at approximately 12:57 PM CDT just north of U.S. Highway 278 and west of Holly Pond near the intersection of County Roads 1650 and 1682. There, it quickly assumed EF1 status, uprooting a hardwood tree, and causing door damage to small farm outbuildings nearby.  The tornado tracked generally northeastward, uprooting and snapping large hardwood trees along County Rd 1683. Farther northeast, near the intersection of County Roads 1709, 1710, and 1711, multiple hardwood trees were snapped and uprooted, and in a small neighborhood there, a house experienced roof damage.  The tornado continued to track generally northeastward across a mix of open farmland and woodland, with snapped and uprooted hardwood trees again observed along County Rd 1716.  To the northeast in the Brooklyn community, the tornado uprooted and snapped hardwood trees along County Rd 1684, and minor roof damage occurred to a single family dwelling. There were also two cattle deaths due to tree falls off of County Rd 1684. The tornado crossed northward on the east side of Brooklyn, and headed farther northeast to east side of Baileyton, where it occasionally snapped and uprooted hardwood trees along the way.  Just to the northeast of Baileyton along County Rd 1762, the tornado caused tree damage, with one large tree falling on and damaging a truck. Roof damage also occurred to a nearby house.  Farther northeast along County Rd 1763, the tornado uprooted hardwood and softwood trees, pushed a mobile home off its foundation, and caused significant roof damage to the dwelling.  The tornado began curving slightly westward as it neared the intersections of Highway 67 and 69, causing sporadic tree damage along the way and also along Apple Grove Rd. The tornado then tracked north-northwestward, ending on County Rd 1589 just west of AL Highway 67 at approximately 1:14 PM CDT.

A tornado developed along Sparks Road, east of Demopolis, near the Marengo County/Hale County line, where several hardwood trees were snapped and uprooted, and a residence had siding damage either from wind or fallen trees. The tornado then moved northeast and impacted homes just off Highway 80 near Yellow Creek Road. Shingles and siding were removed from a couple of homes, a shed was destroyed, and general yard items were strewn. Perhaps the most eye-catching item was the displacement and flipping of a box truck and a pontoon boat. The tornado then crossed Highway 80 with minimal signs of damage and came to an end just past the Hale County line, along Mount Olive Road, where tree branches were broken.

The National Weather Service conducted a storm survey and determined that an EF0 85 mph tornado occurred in southwest Morgantown the evening of Friday, May 22, 2026.

Tree damage was first observed at a farm at the end of Viles Cemetery Road, where several treetops were damaged and pointing in different directions ranging from the southwest to southeast consistent with a convergent pattern from the small tornado.  The damage continued to the east toward Viles Cemetery where some large branches were on the ground.  Nearby Viles Cemetery Road, a field of tall grasses were bent and laying south in the direction of the tornado inflow.

The tornado continued across Gardner Lane where Final Finish Repair Shop sustained extensive roof damage.  The roof was peeled back to the northwest direction, while a lot of insulation was carried eastward into nearby trees and power lines.  Right to the east of Final Finish Repair Shop, the tornado lifted with no additional ground damage.  However, insulation from Final Finish Repair Shop was lofted into nearby fields, across the Natcher Parkway (I-165) and in nearby trees at the Butler County High School Football Stadium.  In total the short lived tornado was 0.32 miles long, although insulation from the Final Finish Repair Shop was observed at least another third of a mile from the end of the tornado as it was carried by the thunderstorm.

The National Weather Service would like to thank Butler County Emergency Management for the assistance with the storm survey.  The National Weather Service would also like to thank the many individuals who sent helpful pictures and video footage of the tornado.

A tornado was observed west of Highway 71 and south of County Road 44 moving due east. This tornado was initially obscured by rain and may have developed further west. The tornado began to curve towards the southeast as it underwent the occlusion process, shrinking from a stovepipe appearance to a rope as it quickly moved over farmlands and turbines. No damage was reported. Additionally a Kimball Emergency Manager searched the area and found no damage. Therefore, the tornado will be rated EFU.
Emergency manager reported a brief tornado to the southeast of Kimball. This tornado lasted about 30 seconds and stayed over open fields.

A large dusty landspout was well documented north of Pine Bluffs. The tornado formed directly under the updraft base of a developing thunderstorm after a boundary collision. Images of this tornado suggested this landspout may have been a hybrid type landspout/tornado. This landspout moved east to southeast over a ridge to the north of Pine Bluffs. An area of inflow winds to the west of the vortex kicked up dirt and dust. No damage was reported.

On Sunday, May 24th, 2026 a developing thunderstorm produced a waterspout that moved onshore in the Villages of Bayport Community. Damage to a single pool cage was noted, and some images show small debris being lofted into the air. Residents in the neighborhood reported and shared images of a few additional structures that sustained minor damage. Additionally, a large tree was also blown over in the community one street over from where the main damage was noted. No additional damage or reports could be located.
Track identified in satellite data. No known damage caused. Time estimated from radar.
Track identified in satellite data. No known damage caused. Time estimated from radar.

The tornado initially touched down just north of U.S. 84 near Cowarts in Houston County, damaging trees and outbuildings. A pool screen was damaged at a home along Omussee Road, with additional tree and minor damage to homes. The tornado damaged the WDHN television station as it crossed Highway 52, breaking windows and damaging the roof. The tornado continued north-northeast downing trees and causing minor structural damage before moving into Henry County at County Road 22 and Buckhead Drive. The most severe damage was along County Road 15 where two homes were heavily damage. One home was destroyed. This home separated from the concrete foundation, slid, and then collapsed. Assessment is ongoing regarding the rating at this location. All other damage is consistent with an EF1 tornado with maximum winds of approximately 105 mph.

Wymore Fire Department and a storm spotter reported a tornado approximately 3 miles northwest of Odell. NWS survey was inconclusive. Tree damage across western Gage County was primarily due to straight line winds from thunderstorms that occurred two days before this event.
Tornado path identified on satellite. No known damage. Time estimated from radar.
Tornado path identified on satellite imagery. No known damage. Time estimated from radar.
Track identified in satellite data. No known damage caused. Time estimated from radar.
Track identified in satellite data. No known damage caused. Time estimated from radar.
Estimated time and location of tornado based on reports received from emergency management and radar interpretation.

A tornado briefly touched down just west of U.S. Hwy 301, where the resident of a home along Loch Ness Gln witnessed damage to the backyard fence. The resident reported that the tornado lifted shortly thereafter, while another area resident witnessed debris being lofted in an open field just to the north prior to the tornado lifting. No additional damage or reports were received.

A tornado moved ashore from the Choctawhatchee Bay into the small village of Villa Tasso. The tornado snapped and uprooted many hardwood trees, primarily on Yacht Club Drive, Robert Avenue, Magnolia Street and Virginia Court. Structural damage was largely due to fallen trees. However, one home on Hal Street suffered damage to about 40% of its roof. The tornado caused two trees to fall on a car at the intersection of Defuniak Street and CR 20 before lifting. Damage along most of the path was consistent with EF-1 damage with maximum winds estimated at 105 mph.
Several storm chasers reported funnel cloud moved across highway 277 and briefly had fully condensed east of the highway for a short time (1 to 3 minutes). small broken tree branches were noted.
Multiple trained spotters reported a brief, weak tornado, supported by photographic evidence. No damage was reported.
Approximate path of weak tornado based on damage reports from the public.

A tornado touched down in an open field southwest of the intersection of 266th St and 459th Ave. The tornado moved to the northeast and across a farmstead where it damaged two barns, downed several large tree limbs, and a fence. The tornado moved northeast across 266th St before lifting in an open field to the north.

The tornado was first visible from a storm chaser livestream in an open field west of 466th Ave and north of 291st St. The tornado moved southeast toward a farmstead at the intersection of 466th Ave and 291st St, where minor tree damage was reported. The primary circulation then broadened and at times exhibited smaller brief vortices. Additional minor tree damage occurred before the tornado lifted in the vicinity of 291st St and 467th Ave.
A brief touchdown in an open field noted by swirling dirt from a storm chaser livestream. No known damage.

A tornado was noted from a storm chaser livestream in an open field south of 263rd St, moving slowly to the northeast. At times, the tornado exhibited smaller brief vortices. The tornado passed over a farmstead along 263rd St, west of 438th Ave, damaging an old barn before lifting.

A very brief tornado rotating around a much larger mesocyclone moved southeast to northwest across Mount Hope Dairy, destroying one barn and damaging another before quickly lifting. Debris from the barns was scattered north of 290th St in a southwest to northeast orientation.

Available Sentinel 2 satellite imagery revealed a weak EF0 tornado occurred in the Isney area. The tornado began south of Wildflower Road, tracking northeast across Poultry Road, causing a roughly 180-yard-wide corridor of tree damage. This tornado also crossed the path of another tornado that occurred near this location back on March 11th of this year along Poultry Road. The tornado lifted just prior to reaching Highway 84. Additional adjustments to this tornado are possible as higher resolution imagery becomes available. Review of additional high resolution satellite imagery revealed the tornado crossed Highway 84 affecting a property to the north of the road damaging a few trees.

Video demonstrated a brief tornado developed over a corn field and toppled an apple tree, and then lifted a well cover into a window. Considering lack of additional damage, the tornado likely lifted in the vicinity of a nearby barn as it moved south-southeastwards.

Damaging winds from a downburst began just south of Landmark Elementary School along Russenberger Rd. The swath of wind continued south/southeastward for 8.8 miles, with a maximum width of 4.6 miles. Damage was spotty in nature along and mostly to the
west of I530. Most of the damage was isolated to uprooted trees in 1 to 2 tree clusters. Additionally several power lines were found to be damaged, most of this damage was caused by tree-fall with a couple of downed polls from wind itself. 1 structure was damaged due to a tree uprooting and landing on the structure.
Peak wind speed was estimated to be 80 mph along Dreher Rd with sporadic 60-75 mph winds found along the path.

A severe thunderstorm produced a swath of 60-75 mph wind extending from just east of Hartwell to far northeast Elbert County. The damaging wind swath began near Hart State Park and Ridge Road where numerous trees were downed. The highest wind gusts of 75 mph were estimated along Old 29 Hwy and Elrod Ferry Road where dozens of trees were downed, including several onto homes. 60-70 mph gusts continued south across Hwy 29 and crossed into Elbert County in the Montevideo area. A church in the Rock Branch community sustained roof damage with a portion of sheet metal peeled off. The strongest gusts subsided as the storm moved down Ruckersville Road.

Available Sentinel 2 satellite imagery revealed an EF1 tornado occurred in the Smyer area off of Highway 69. The tornado remained solely within forest staying just east of Highway 69. It tracked northeast for approximately 3 miles causing a 100-yard-wide corridor of tree damage. Additional adjustments to this tornado are possible as higher resolution imagery becomes available.

Available Sentinel 2 satellite imagery revealed that an EF1 tornado tracked across forested parts of Clarke County in the Campbell area just west of Highway 69. The tornado remained solely within the forest, causing an approximately 250 yard wide corridor of tree damage. The tornado lifted just prior to reaching Wood Bluff Road. Additional adjustments to this tornado are possible as higher resolution imagery becomes available.
Path estimated from radar data. An Emergency Management official reported a brief tornado in open fields with dust and dirt being kicked up. No damage was noted.

Emergency Management and storm chaser videos documented a brief tornado. Location is estimated based on radar information. The tornado lasted approximately 30 seconds before dissipating. No damage was reported.

A landspout tornado was reported to the west of Iron Mountain. A narrow funnel cloud is visible in media along with a dust column extending most of the way from the ground to the funnel. Location is estimated from media. No damage was reported.

A third landspout was observed to have lasted longer than 10 minutes. A narrow funnel was well documented to the east-southwest of Farthing. A dust column extended up to the funnel. No damage was reported.

A diffused ground circulation with a small funnel cloud was documented by a storm chaser to the west of Highway 71. At the surface a large area of dust underneath this funnel was slowly rotating. The tornado lasted less than a minute.
A second landspout touched down shortly after the first dissipated. This one remained over rough terrain and did no damage.
This very short-lived tornado damaged some stands of trees. A TDS was observed via radar during this time.

This tornado developed along Hoff Road, west of Highway 71 and north of School House Road. It moved north-northwest crossing Hoff Cutoff and Nickletown Road, and then dissipated south of Palestine Road. The tornado uprooted trees, damaged a couple outbuildings, and snapped numerous large tree limbs.

This tornado developed along Watson Road, west of Highway 71 and north of Young Ridge Road. It moved northwest across Vineyard Creek Road, Hendrix Road, and Nickletown Road, before dissipating just south of Highway 10. The tornado uprooted trees, damaged an outbuilding, and snapped numerous large tree limbs.

This tornado developed in a large corn field north of Gun Club Road and east of Highway 59. It moved north-northwest across Hollis Lake Road where a few trees were uprooted and numerous large tree limbs were snapped. It then moved across an oxbow lake, crossed Hale Farm Road, and dissipated.

Tree debris from a EF0 tornado was visible along Farm Road 131 southeast of Battlefield, MO. Eyewitness account depicted the tornado as it crossed Plainview Road at James Road. Additionally, Sentinel-2 satellite data analysis revealed some tree damage just outside of the Rivercut Golf Course. Max winds were estimated at 70 mph with a width of 50 yards.

Reports and videos of a brief, dusty tornado southeast of Bowbells. Tornado fully formed around 8:50 PM and soon after knocked over a grain bin and sheared off the top half of pine trees. The tornado then tracked to the northeast for a couple of miles before dissipating before reaching the river.

A strong line of storms crossed over the Monongahela River at around 2:49pm on June 6th. An embedded meso-vortex developed in the line with tightening rotation around 2:50pm, when the tornado is estimated to have touched down in Linn near Railroad Avenue. Time was estimated from radar. The strongest winds accelerated on the southern end of the vortex as it moved downhill into Redstone Creek Valley. Winds on the southern end of the vortex and northern end of the rear flank downdraft were the strongest, estimated at 100mph with a large amount of small hardwood trees down. The strongest winds were along Braznell Concrete Road, just northeast of its intersection with Taylor Flats Road. Some shingle damage was noted on a home before it ended. The vortex collapsed, along with a weakening of the rear flank downdraft push around 2:51pm after crossing Braznell Concrete Road one more time.
Estimated location and path of tornado. A white rope tornado came down and was on the ground for about 3 minutes... kicking up dust. No damage reported so EF-Unknown rating assigned.

On June 6th, a brief EF-1 tornado occurred just southwest of Beallsville, originating from a meso-vortex within a broad line of storms that impacted the region. Initial damage, consisting of several large snapped branches and uprooted trees, was observed along Kefover Road. A farm on Glendon Lane became a primary area of focus after a barn was partially destroyed, with debris scattered northeastward across a field and onto a neighboring property; the fact that this debris was lofted to the left of the storm's general path served as an indicator of rotation. This location also saw a line of trees uprooted at a valley base and several pines snapped mid-trunk, though the residence sustained only minor porch damage. As the storm moved eastward up the hillside, it left sporadic tree damage in its wake before causing further concentrated destruction along Martindale Road, where numerous trees were snapped or uprooted at a farm and adjacent site.

A strong line of storms with embedded mesovortices moved across Washington county on June 6th. As the storm was approaching Centerville, the vortex tightened as noted on radar. This coincides with a swath of damage to trees from just west of Conti Road to Spring Road, with nearly 200 trees down around the National Pike Steam Show property. Trees were both snapped and uprooted, indicative of 95-100mph wind.

A strong line of storms entered northern Fayette County, crossing Route 51 at around 2:56pm on June 6th. At the same time, it was evident that an embedded meso-vortex developed based on radar; this rotation extended to the surface resulting in an estimated tornado touchdown near Reservoir Road just east-southeast of Star Junction at 2:57pm. Time was estimated from radar. Damage continued, coincident with the vortex, and just south of the vortex for around 5.1 miles. Damage was sporadic at times, the tornado may have lifted and re-formed multiple times. Most damage was hardwood trees uprooted along Maplewood Road, Virgin Run Road, and Dickerson Run Road. The strongest damage was estimated at 90mph along Maplewood Road, just west of its intersection with Virgin Run Road where multiple hardwood trees were down with shingle damage to a home at around 2:58pm. The tornado continued, crossing the ridgetop just west of Dickerson Run road where drone footage shows a narrow swath of convergent tree damage, before the vortex continued across multiple fields, ending near Cemetery Road just north of Vanderbilt at 3:02pm.

On the afternoon of June 6, 2026, an EF1 tornado, generated within a squall line, tracked just over 7 miles eastward across Washington County, PA. The tornado first formed near Cokeburg, snapping large pine trees between Route 917 and Washington Street. After a brief lift, it reformed two miles east near Ellsworth, along Beallsville Road and Cherry Street. This segment recorded the highest intensity, with maximum wind gusts of 110 mph. Damage included the snapping of approximately 50 hardwood trees and partial roof damage to one home on Cherry Street from a falling tree. The tornado continued its path, primarily snapping or uprooting hardwood trees as it crossed Deems Park Road, Woodland Road, Locust Road, Scenic Drive, California Drive, and Deer Run Lane, before finally dissipating at Cross Ridge Road.

A brief EF1 tornado struck the northern border of Fayette County, Pennsylvania, on the afternoon of June 6, 2026, originating within a squall line. The tornado was active for four to five minutes, starting its track between Banning and Layton in Fayette County. Following a path that included Banning Road, Cross Road, and Boy Scout Road, the tornado’s wind gusts, which peaked between 95 and 110 mph, snapped and uprooted numerous large hardwood trees. The damage extended to remote locations, as aerial video provided by the South Huntington Township volunteer fire department later confirmed. The tornado dissipated in southern Westmoreland County where Meadow Run Road and Epsey Road meet.

An NWS survey team confirmed a short, narrow path of tree damage consistent with an EF0 tornado between Spokane and Highlandville in Christian County. Additionally, Sentinel-2 satellite data analysis revealed tree damage at the start of the track near Camp Creek, southwest of Stoneshire Drive.

This tornado was embedded within a larger area of wind damage and produced areas of tree damage from just southeast of SE 44th St and Bryant Road to along SE 47th Street east of Sooner Road, or just west of Tinker AFB.

An NWS survey team concluded that a tornado developed just east of Sparta and moved to the northeast. A wide tract of uprooted trees and large tree limbs fell in a cyclonic pattern spanning the path, where a tornado debris signature was observed on radar. A mobile home and a single-family home were found to be damaged.

A landspout was photographed by multiple vantages to the south of Lyman. A light colored dust column extended up to the clouds associated with a boundary. The landspout was short-lived and likely remained over fields during its duration. Location is estimated from media and no damage was reported.
Intermittent track, mainly topping trees

Large mesocyclone slowly moved southeastward across western Dickinson County. Widespread wind damage was noted well outside of the tornadic region due to the strong low-level mesocyclone. Tree branches broken and corn flattened in a convergent pattern on the periphery of the overall circulation, with several enhanced areas of damage within the tornadic centerline. Tornado path was likely internment due to transient nature of individual tornadic vortices.

At approximately 5:15 AM, a brief tornado developed east of Weeping Water, just north of South Cedar Creek. The tornado produced sporadic tree damage, with estimated wind speeds of 65 to 74 mph. The tornado dissipated near South Cedar Creek at approximately 5:16 AM.
Track based on input from chasers who witnessed the short track tornado in this area.

The National Weather Service Cleveland conducted a storm damage survey in cooperation with the Lorain County Emergency Management Agency following severe thunderstorms that moved through Lorain County on the evening of Wednesday, June 10, 2026. The survey determined that a microbursts produced significant straight-line wind damage across central Amherst between approximately 8:23 PM to 8:24 PM EDT.

The a microburst occurred around 8:23 PM and affected portions of central Amherst near Cleveland Avenue and areas just west of South Leavitt Road. Damage included siding torn from a building along Cleveland Avenue, two large trees uprooted along Cleveland Avenue, and several large tree limbs falling onto a detached garage west of South Leavitt Road. In addition, more than 30 large tree limbs were snapped or broken throughout the damaged path. The damage pattern was consistent with divergent winds associated with a microburst.

Based on the extent and severity of the damage observed during the survey, peak wind speeds were estimated at up to 85 mph in the strongest portions of the microbursts. The National Weather Service Cleveland extends its appreciation to the Lorain County EMA for providing transportation assistance and participating in the storm survey. Their support was instrumental in documenting the damage and completing the assessment.

The National Weather Service Cleveland conducted a storm damage survey in cooperation with the Lorain County Emergency Management Agency following severe thunderstorms that moved through Lorain County on the evening of Wednesday, June 10, 2026. The survey determined that a microbursts produced significant straight-line wind damage across northeast  Amherst around 8:30 PM EDT.

A microburst occurred around 8:30 PM in the northeastern portion of Amherst. The most concentrated damage was observed north of State Route 2 and near North Ridge Road, including the Cooper Foster Park Road West corridor. Thunderstorm wind gusts overturned a storage container, snapped a utility pole, and knocked down a restaurant sign along Cooper Foster Park Road West. Two large trees were uprooted and fell across Cooper Foster Park Road West, and an additional seven trees were uprooted in the surrounding area. Approximately 50 tree limbs were also downed onto power lines, homes, and roadways. As with the first area of damage, an additional seven trees were uprooted in the surrounding area. Approximately 50 tree limbs were also downed onto power lines, homes, and roadways. As with the first area of damage, the observed pattern was consistent with a microburst producing strong divergent winds.

Based on the extent and severity of the damage observed during the survey, peak wind speeds were estimated at up to 85 mph in the strongest portions of the microbursts. The National Weather Service Cleveland extends its appreciation to the Lorain County EMA for providing transportation assistance and participating in the storm survey. Their support was instrumental in documenting the damage and completing the assessment.

At approximately 5:10 AM, a tornado developed just northeast of Weeping Water near Brittini Drive and moved southeast. The tornado produced sporadic tree damage before causing the complete collapse of the walls of a farm building near Weeping Water Road and 124th Street. Based on this damage, peak winds were estimated around 100 mph. Additional tree damage was also noted on the property. The tornado dissipated before reaching Weeping Water Creek at approximately 5:14 AM.
Multiple chasers and spotter reported a brief tornado in this approximate location.  No damage was found, so the tornado will be rated an EF-U.
Law enforcement reported a brief tornado in an open field near Henry. Emergency Manager confirmed with land owners and via Search and Rescue drone footage that no damage occurred from the tornado.
Two videos of a very narrow needle-like tornado north of Ainsworth in a field.  The mesocyclone appeared to be very small as well.  With no known damage, this is rated as an EFU tornado.
Video and photos of a small tornado were provided and minor damage was noted on a storm survey in the vicinity of where the photo and video were taken.

At approximately 5:21 AM, a brief tornado developed northeast of Nehawka, Nebraska, near 12th Street and Beccard Drive, and moved southeast. The tornado caused fairly extensive tree damage at a residence, including several large broken branches. Based on this damage, peak winds were estimated around 90 mph. The tornado continued southeast, producing additional sporadic tree damage with estimated winds of 65 to 74 mph, before dissipating near 6th Avenue and Hoback Road at approximately 5:24 AM.
Chaser video of short lived condensation funnel on the ground.  No known damage, rated as an EFU.

At approximately 5:33 AM, a brief tornado developed north of Tabor, Iowa, and moved east. The tornado produced sporadic tree damage near 235th Street and Pathfield Road, with estimated winds around 65 mph. Shortly after this damage occurred, KOAX radar displayed a tornadic debris signature associated with the tornado. The tornado was estimated to have a maximum width of 20 yards. The tornado dissipated at approximately 5:35 AM.
EFU tornado based on video and photos relayed to NWS through Emergency Management and broadcast media. No damage reported by EMA and local fire department.
This tornado touched down along Kent St. west of Athens, and tracked southeast to Fitschen Rd. on the south edge of Athens. A number of trees were snapped along the path.

A weak tornado touched down in a field northwest of a tree line west of County Road 675N. It then crossed another tree line and traveled through a corn field with drone footage revealing a clear circulation and path within the corn. It then impacted a home north of the intersection of County Road 675N and 100N. It pushed and rotated an RV, ripped off an awning and ripped a 500 gallon propane tank off the concrete block. The drone footage then shows the circulation ends east of 675W.

Brief tornado began on the south side of 18th street west of 72nd Ave. Two barn outbuilding structures were heavily damaged with metal roofing lofted and deposited several hundred yards downwind. Several trees were damaged, uprooted, or received large limbs damage. Tree limbs with damage toward the end of the track along 72nd Ave were blown and deposited across the street.

Drone footage provided by Cass County Emergency Management confirmed an EF-1 tornado occurred within a line of severe thunderstorms across northeast Cass County. The tornado began just south of County Road 325 N between County Road 400 E and 450 E where the roof of a barn was damaged. The tornado then tracked northeast and produced noticeable scouring of crops. The tornado destroyed a 40ft pole barn on County Road 375 N and caused additional damage to the roofs of barns along County Road 500 E. The tornado dissipated by County Road 425 N where some minor tree damage was observed.
Damage to numerous trees, a few uprooted. Barn damaged with roof decking blown across the intersection of County Road V and F.

This tornado appeared to touch down just west of Hendricks Street and moved eastward through central Merrillville. Numerous homes sustained significant damage along W 64rd Ave, 61st Pl, 61st Ave, and Grand Pl, including removal of walls and roofing structures. Extensive tree damage was noted in this region, as well. The tornado continued eastward along and just north of W 61st Avenue and moved over Andrean High School, causing significant roofing damage. Thereafter, the tornado crossed Interstate 65 and then moved over S Liverpool Road, causing continued damage to trees. The tornado then tracked into the southwestern side of Hobart before lifting just southwest of W 3rd Street.

The tornado developed just east of the Illinois River, mainly damaging trees as it tracked northeast over northwest Woodford county.  The tornado strengthened in the Columbia road area, where several houses lost roofs and extensive tree damage was observed.  The tornado reached peak intensity (EF3) northwest of Washburn in rural areas of southern Marshall County.  Here, a log house had all walls collapsed and a nearby house lost its roof and second floor.  Severe tree damage was seen here, where some trees had only trunks and large branches remaining.  Extensive crop damage was also noted, with corn leaves ripped off and plants uprooted.  Tornado width was measured at 930 yards at this point with estimated peak winds of 155 mph.  The tornado continued east, gradually weakening while damaging trees, outbuildings, and damaging roofs of a few more houses.  It dissipated in a farm field northeast of Washburn.

This tornado formed roughly at the intersection of 98th Avenue and Sheffield Avenue and then proceeded to track northeastward through St. John. Most of the damage along the tornado's roughly 5.5 mile track was confined to trees, but some roof damage was also noted, and one house also had its garage door and side wall blown out. The tornado dissipated just east of Rohrman Park shortly after crossing into Schererville.

Eyewitness reports and radar data indicate that a tornado began in Pratt's Wayne Woods before quickly intensifying and tracking east-northeastward into Bartlett. The tornado produced a concentrated area of EF-1 damage at a shopping center at the intersection of Sutton Road and Stearns Road, where roofing material was peeled off of buildings, brick columns and metal fencing were blown out at a garden center, and all of the gas pumps at a gas station were blown over. The tornado continued to produce extensive tree damage in the subdivisions to the east of the shopping center before dissipating east of Bartlett Road.

The tornado spun up 3 miles northeast of Tallula, damaging a grain bin and several trees at a farmstead on Reimer Ave. It continued tracking east-northeast, damaging several trees and removing shingles from a home on State Park Rd and Lincoln New Salem Park. It crossed IL Route 97, damaging more trees in a neighborhood just south of the Athens Blacktop Rd. It then lifted 1 mile southwest of Tice before ending just before 11 pm CDT.

A brief tornado spun up south of 8A on King Rd, uprooting or snapping multiple trees and causing damage to a barn. The tornado continued northeast, flipping a center pivot before entering a grove of trees causing several snapped trees. The circulation moved quickly northeast, knocking down a few more trees north of 8A Rd. The tornado quickly lifted on the north side of 8A Rd after doing significant damage to a barn.
Damage in a short path to the northeast across Lomira include several homes/mobile homes with roof damage, trees uprooted and limbs snapped.

Drone photographs taken by a trained spotter show a tornado path began in a field approximately two miles southwest of Ipava, just north of the east-west oriented portion of north County Highway 12. Drone footage of the tornado showed it continued northeast, impacting a solar farm and tossing a few solar panels. It produced some crop damage in the fields and continued towards Ipava, crossing Bernadotte Street just south of west Main Street. Video shows a very weak tornado continued across Ipava, and there was no damage evident in the footage. The tornado dissipated on the northeast side of Ipava, near the intersection of Kinsey and Mechanic Street, prior to reaching the open field.

Drone footage provided by Jay County Emergency Management confirmed a brief EF-0 tornado occurred within a line of severe thunderstorms across northwest Jay County. The tornado began just south of 550 N where a barn had the roof blown off. There was also some roof damage to a nearby house and several trees were snapped off. Debris was lofted well northeast into the nearby fields. Debris was observed all the way to State Road 1 where additional minor tree and roof damage was observed. The tornado dissipated shortly after crossing State Road 1.

A tornado touched down in the vicinity of W 400 S and S 300 W on the southwest edge of Wabash. At this location, a number of wood power poles were snapped at the base. The tornado then raced northeast to Glendale Dr., McKibben St., and Barkley Dr. in Wabash where a number of homes of damaged. Homes lost shingles or even portions of the roof decking. Debris was lofted into nearby tree lines. One dual-axle fifth-wheel camper was tipped over. Insulation and dirt splatter was noted at a few different homes. Beyond Berkley Dr., damage was limited to instances of small limbs down in the neighborhood. Farther northeast, in the vicinity of Lafountaine Ave and W Waterworks Rd., an outbuilding was destroyed when its south-facing door appeared to be blown, in resulting in a collapse of walls and loss of roof panels. The tornado reached its peak intensity as it moved over properties on W Water Works road. Here, two injuries were reported as homes lost windows and roof decking, and a manufactured home was shifted several feet off its foundation. Dirt and insulation splatter was noted in these areas. Beyond S Meridian Rd., damage was once again limited to instances of trees or branches down. Powerlines were down near E Baumbauer Rd, where the tornado appears to have lifted.

The tornado appeared to start near IL Route 23 just north of Rowe
before tracking northeastward across portions of central Livingston 
County. The tornado may not have been fully condensed to the ground 
or consisted of intermittent touchdowns along the first two thirds
of the path with damage primarily confined to trees. Based on storm 
chaser videos, the tornado appeared to rapidly strengthen and widen
while crossing Route 47 and approaching the unincorporated community 
of Blair where several homesteads sustained roof and siding damage 
and several barns were destroyed. Storm chaser video depicted subvortices
within the tornado as it crossed several open fields in the general 
area. The tornado then appeared to lift just north of Route 17. The
tornado was likely stronger than the  official rating of EF1, though 
a lack of damage indicators precludes a higher rating.

The tornado touched down west of Campbell road and impacted several farm buildings along Campbell road. One of the farm buildings was completely destroyed with debris scattered into an open field to the east. The tornado then mostly traveled over farm fields in eastern Johnson county before impacting two homes along Rocklane Road. Debris from a damaged outbuilding near the first home on Rocklane Road was picked up and thrown about 650 yards to the northeast. The tornado continued into Shelby county where it impacted one home along West 525 North before traveling through open fields and impacting one additional home on 600W. The tornado then tracked mostly through open fields, impacting a home south of Clover Village before it crossed Interstate 74 and passed harmlessly through several additional fields. There was another concentrated area of damage near 75W and 600N where widespread tree damage and minor home damage was noted. It then dissipated in an open field near Hill Branch Creek. The tornado may have lifted briefly along the path.

Drone footage revealed clear convergence within a grove of trees south of a home south of West County Road 122 North. The tree damage began and ended within a grove of trees with little to no damage to nearby properties.

A supercell thunderstorm produced its first tornado north of Weatherby in Dekalb County along NE Irwin Road.  It traveled to the east-northeast and crossed into Daviess County north of Alta Vista.  The tornado traveled generally along Route KK before dissipating a couple of miles west of Interstate 35.  The tornado primarily produced minor to moderate tree damage on its path, consistent with spotter reports.

A long-track tornado initially touched down near the intersection of Grand Boulevard and Clay Street just east of Interstate 65 in rural Lake County and continued northeastward into southern Porter County just north of the Kankakee River. Damage near the beginning of the path consisted of downed and uprooted trees. The tornado appeared to increase in size and intensity after crossing US Highway 231, damaging the walls and roofing of several homes near W 1000 S just north of Breyfogel Ditch.

As the tornado continued northeastward, it further strengthened and widened. The tornado reached its peak intensity of EF-3 from just north of Kouts to just west of the Porter and LaPorte county line. In this area, several homes were destroyed, and two separate sets of high tension power trusses were sheared apart and collapsed. There was significant scouring of the ground and damage to crops in this region, as well. The tornado began to weaken as it crossed into LaPorte County, where drone footage continued to show swirl marks in fields as it tracked northeast and eventually turned toward the north-northeast. The tornado then dissipated after damaging trees and residences along S 1050 W Road.

This tornado began near Colfax Street northeast of Schneider and caused mainly tree damage along its northeastward track, consistent with EF-0 winds near 85 mph. The tornado appears to have crossed I-65 north of E 205th Avenue. It continued into Porter County before lifting just south of Hebron.

A tornado developed southwest of Andrews, racing northeast toward Huntington. At least two properties on W Division Rd were impacted, as indicated by a loss of shingles, siding, and roof panels. Numerous trees were damaged as well, including trees snapped. Near the intersection of W 100 N and N 800 W, additional tree damage was observed and an outbuilding lost several roof panels. Along W 200 N, a number of trees were damaged at one property. Across the street, a mobile home lost its roof. The tornado appears to have lifted prior to reaching the Yake Subdivision, just south of the Wabash River. In the subdivision, isolated tree branches were down.
A brief, likely rain-wrapped, EF-0 tornado occurred on the west side of Galt, damaging trees and a few grain bins in a mostly west-to-east path.

A tornado touched down north of Pleasant Plain, at a residence on S 500 W. Here, nearly two dozen trees were damaged, including multiple trees snapped at least halfway up their trunks. Tree damage appeared to continue into a tree line off to the northeast. Throughout its nearly 8-mile long path to the northeast, sporadic instances of tree damage occurred until it approached State Route 5, just northwest of I-69. Here, the tornado caused almost total destruction to a newly built barndominium. Only the eastern wall was left standing with debris lofted at least 100 yards into adjacent fields. Tree damage continued east-northeast of here where at least two tree trunks were snapped. The tornado lifted just east of I-69, along S 200 E. Many thanks to Huntington County Emergency Management who helped document this tornado path.

Video footage captured this tornado forming along W 151st Avenue west of Parrish Avenue. It tracked northeast into the adjacent Lynnsway subdivision on the southwest side of Cedar Lake, where it caused minor roofing and siding damage to multiple houses and lofted trash cans and outdoor furniture into the air. The tornado then tracked east-northeastward for a few miles through the south side of Cedar Lake, primarily producing tree damage before dissipating near the Pheasant Valley Country Club.

The tornado touched down about a half mile south of Highway 9 east of county road 1300E, overturning an irrigation pivot. It crossed Highway 1 on the south edge of town and damaged the roof of a tractor dealership. It skirted the south edge of Hoopeston, causing damage to trees and shingles. It strengthened by the time it reached the intersection of Highway 9 and 1700E, snapping tree trunks and damaging the roof of a house. Down the road, an outbuilding was flattened, and several additional trees were snapped. It entered Cheneyville and snapped additional tree trunks; significant damage to buildings at the intersection of Highway 9 and 1900E was likely due to rear-flank downdraft winds up to 100 mph. The tornado appears to have lifted before reaching the Indiana border.

This tornado touched down about 1.5 miles south of Groveland, and moved northeast along the southern edge of Morton. A number of tree trunks were snapped, a few of which fell onto cars. It left town near the intersection of Jefferson St. and Tennessee Ave. and entered the Mayfair subdivision, causing extensive tree limb damage and damage to some shingles. It crossed I-74 about 1.5 miles east of the Washington Rd. overpass. Along Harding Rd., it impacted a couple of farmsteads, damaging an outbuilding at one of them. The tornado crossed into Woodford County about 1 mile north of Deer Creek, before lifting near county road 1200E.

In an open area north of US 24 and east of State Route 9, an incredibly brief tornado appears to have touched down and impacted a single residence. Here, a two-story home completely lost its roof and debris was deposited into adjacent fields. Hardly any rafters remain and no roof decking is present. Intense dirt and insulation splatter was noted on the east and north side of the home. Additionally, a detached garage to the south-southeast of the home was demolished by the tornado. A property less then 500 yards to the northeast was not impacted, suggesting the tornado quickly lifted beyond 600 N.

The tornado began about 3 mile west of the Springfield Capital Airport where it lofted 6,000-lb aircraft hangars and rolled an enclosed trailer. Some of the most significant damage was at the Animal  Protective League animal shelter on Taintor Road. The tornado continued east-southeast, producing tree and building damage around Camp Butler and through Mechanicsburg, damaging several farm outbuildings and trees along its path. It ended about 5 miles east of Mechanicsburg just north of the Sangamon River.

This tornado touched down along N Duncan Rd near I-74 and Hwy 150 where it damaged solar panels, fencing and a few trees. It progressed across I-74 where it damaged the roof of a business and toppled a small metal tower along N Mattis Ave. The tornado progressed east and produced tree damage as well as additional roof damage to a warehouse. The tornado produced additional tree damage and an outbuilding damage as it progressed along W Oaks Rd N.  The tornado crossed Hwy 45 just northeast of Frasca Field and then  largely tracked east. Structural damage was mainly some roof damage close to Hwy 45, with a number of trees snapped further east.

This tornado touched down about a third of a mile south of the Champaign and Ford County line, along County Road 2000. It peeled part of the roof off an outbuilding, and damaged some solar panels. It crossed the border about a quarter mile west of Ford County Road 2800E, causing significant damage at a farmstead. Here, the main residence lost part of its roof, an outbuilding was nearly destroyed, and a number of trees were snapped. It lifted a short time later, after crossing 2280E.

This tornado largely paralleled I-74 to the north. Some outbuildings were significantly damaged near the start of the track, but the greatest damage was in Kickapoo State Recreation Area. Here, an estimated 250 trees were snapped or damaged by winds up to 110 mph. The tornado lifted along Hungry Hollow Rd., just before moving into Danville. Damage in Danville itself was determined to be from straight-line winds of 80 to 100 mph.

A brief tornado developed just east of the Missouri River at approximately 5:29 AM. The tornado produced minor tree damage as it tracked east towards Interstate 29. As the tornado reached Interstate 29, the tornado intensified. EF1 damage was produced at a residence located along Western Ave with most of the roof lifted off this residence. The tornado then crossed Interstate 29 and produced tree damage along the interstate before dissipating at approximately 5:31 AM.

At approximately 5:58 AM, a tornado developed just east of Coburg, Iowa, near 105th Street and K Avenue, and moved east-southeast. The tornado produced sporadic tree damage with an estimated wind speeds of 70 mph. The tornado would then track east, parallel to 110th St. Along the path, trees and farm outbuildings received damage. Max wind speeds were estimated at low-end EF1 intensity of 90 mph. The tornado would dissipate at approximately 6:08 AM  near 110th St and R Ave. The estimated max width was approximately 100 yards.

A brief tornado developed south of Villisca at approximately 6:11 AM. The tornado would track along 110th St between V Ave and Willow Ave before dissipating near the county line at 6:13 AM. Along the tornado's path, trees were damaged, a farm outbuilding lost part of the roof and wall, and a carport was destroyed. The tornado had estimated wind speeds of 90 mph earning a rating of EF1. The maximum estimated width of the tornado was approximately 50 yards.

This tornado began approximately one and half miles southwest of Boswell, initially damaging an outbuilding and peeling a few roof shingles off of a house at a farmstead on S 400 W Road. The tornado tracked east-northeastward and blew down a barn and power lines along S 200 W Road before curving off more towards the northeast. It then blew a press box off of the bleachers at Daugherty Speedway and into a nearby power pole and field before reaching peak intensity as it tracked into the unincorporated community of Chase. There, a grain elevator and multiple associated grain bins were destroyed, and a couple of tree trunks were snapped. The tornado then continued to the east-northeast, snapping multiple rows of power poles from Meridian Road to S 200 E Road and downing another set of power poles in the unincorporated community of Atkinson. As the tornado reached E 200 S and S 600 E roads, it downed more power poles; downed a few trees; damaged the roof, chimney, and gutter of a house; and blew a chicken coop into a field, killing 30 chickens. The tornado likely dissipated shortly after crossing S 600 E Road.

A tornado embedded within a line of severe thunderstorms developed Thursday night in extreme southeast LaGrange County. Around Taylor Lake and Lake of the Woods, damage to electrical poles, along with impressive tree damage in spots, was determined to be consistent with an EF-1 rating, with maximum winds estimated at 90 mph. The tornado then raced northeastward into Steuben County. As the parent cell merged with another portion of the line, the tornado took a more easterly turn, impacting portions of western and northern Angola. Much of the damage along the path was inflicted on trees, suggesting the tornado may have occasionally lifted off the surface. Special thanks to Steuben County Emergency Management for their assistance with this survey.

An EF-0 tornado with peak winds of around 80 mph, a path length of around 1.3 miles, and a maximum width of around 150 yards began near the intersection of Gartner Road and Olesen Drive and continued northeast through the Huntington Hills and Olesen Estates neighborhoods of Naperville. Damage through both neighborhoods was in a very narrow path of around 50 to 75 yards and consisted of snapped and uprooted trees. The tornado appeared to broaden in width while crossing Naper Boulevard and passing over Huntington Apartments, where a roughly 150-yard-wide swath of extensive tree damage was noted. The tornado appeared to lift just west of Benedictine Parkway.

A brief EF-0 tornado with maximum winds estimated at 75 mph touched down on the far southwest side of Argos in Marshall County. Damage along the path was largely confined to trees. Special thanks to the Marshall County EMA and Argos FD for assisting with the survey.

During the evening of Saturday June 13, 2026 a line of damaging thunderstorms moved across the Kansas City Metropolitan Area. At 8:33 PM CDT, a tornado formed on the leading edge of the line near Avondale, MO. The tornado produced sporadic tree damage near the Harrah's Casino before moving over the Missouri River. Sporadic tree damage was found near Birmingham, MO before the tornado crossed the Missouri River near MO-291 and produced substantial tree damage in LaBenite Park. The track could not be followed east of the park and no more damage was found further, so the tornado likely ended east of the park around 8:50 PM CDT. Thank you to Sugar Creek PD for their assistance with the damage survey.

Another tornado, perhaps from the same parent circulation that spawned the Argos tornado, developed on the northeast side of Bourbon in Marshall County. The tornado touched down in a field, with tree damage observed in the distance just east of Beech Road and north of 10B Road. The tornado raced northeastward, striking a property where two old barns collapsed and a third was damaged. Metal roofing material was also blown off, and several trees sustained major damage, consistent with an EF-1 rating. The tornado then crossed the county line into Kosciusko County, where it impacted multiple Amish properties. In this area, a camper was flipped, several softwood trees were snapped, and maximum winds were estimated at 90 to 100 mph.

During the evening of Saturday June 13, 2026 a line of damaging thunderstorms moved across the Kansas City Metropolitan Area. At 8:47 PM CDT, a tornado formed on the leading edge of the line in Liberty, MO. The tornado produced sporadic tree damage as it moved northeast through multiple residential areas and farm fields. The tornado lifted at 8:54 PM CDT approximately 2 miles east of Liberty.

The thunderstorm that developed the Lucerne - Terra Haute EF2 tornado southwest of Unionville continued northeast across Putnam County. Minor, sporadic tree damage was noted along the track of the mesocyclone into northeast Putnam County. The only damage of note was to a single family residence and one outbuilding. Minor tree damage was noted as well. The convergent damage noted was consistent with that of a brief EF0 tornado that likely developed around 4:49 PM CDT and ended at 4:51 PM CDT. Wood frame and corrugated steel construction of the home was noted, with numerous complete roof panels missing.

Wednesday night, June 10th, 2026, an EF0 tornado developed at 6:36 PM CDT. west of US Highway 63 near Sugar Creek Conservation Area. This tornado continued east-northeast across open country, with minor damage noted to a solar panel array and trees before crossing US 63 and across open country north of Millard, MO, and south of Hwy 6. Storm chasers reported visuals of the tornado and were observed via livestreams by NWS meteorologists. Damage survey confirmed an EF-0 tornado.

An EF-2 tornado with peak winds of around 120 mph, a path length of around 8.4 miles, and a maximum width of 350 yards began in the Spears-Pioneer Woods Forest Preserve north of 95th St. and continued northeast into northern Hickory Hills, where tree damage and some light pole damage occurred. The tornado strengthened in intensity to EF-2 level on the southeast side of Justice, where two apartments had roofs fully removed near 83rd St. and Roberts Rd. The tornado maintained EF-2 strength into Bridgeview, where additional roof damage was noted near 79th St. and Oketo Ave. The tornado then weakened as it moved into the Clearing and Garfield Ridge community areas of Chicago west of Midway Airport, where tree, shingle, roof, and siding damage occurred. The tornado lifted north of Midway Airport around 52nd St. and Leamington Ave. after producing additional tree damage.

This tornado began approximately 3 miles southeast of Saybrook in McLean County, where it downed a few tree branches and peeled back the metal roof of an outbuilding. The tornado crossed into Ford County shortly thereafter, where it initially damaged trees, power lines, and an outbuilding in the unincorporated community of Harpster. The tornado then impacted a campground along E 200N Road 2 miles south of Gibson City, where it rolled over and damaged several campers. Trees and farm outbuildings were also damaged at a farmstead one mile east of the campground. The tornado then tracked east-northeastward for a few more miles, primarily producing tree damage before dissipating approximately one mile south-southwest of Elliott.

On Wednesday afternoon, June 10th, 2026, a severe thunderstorm resulted in an EF2 tornado developing south of Lucerne, Missouri, in southwest Putnam County. This tornado began at 3:57 PM CDT, causing minor damage to a home on 212th Street, destroying two empty grain bins, and damaging four outbuildings. Corrugated steel damage was deposited north and northeast across an open farm field toward County Road 455. Tree damage was found toward Terre Haute, MO, before the tornado intensified to EF2, causing significant damage and destruction to an expansive pole barn and two of three large grain bins near the intersection of County Road 469 and 470. The tornado continued northeast toward the intersection of 190th Street and County Road 391, here damage to an older outbuilding was surveyed. The tornado continued east along 190th Street resulting in EF1 damage to an outbuilding and trees before turning slightly southeast and strengthening back to EF2 near State Highway EE and 190th Street. Here the tornado destroyed a mobile home, with estimated max wind speeds of 125 mph. The tornado continued east causing damage to trees north of 190th Street before ending south of US Highway 136 as it crossed East Locust Creek. Special thanks to Missouri SEMA, Putnam County EM, and Putnam County commissioners office for assistance with the survey.

Drone footage from Cass County Emergency Management shows evidence of a tornado southeast of Lake Cicott. Dozens, if not hundreds, of trees were damaged by the brief tornado along with instances of property damage. The tornado appears to have begun over a wooded area near the termination of S CR 750 W (South of W CR 50 S). Here, a few trees were uprooted followed by an area of trees snapped near the base. Based on a convergent signature, the tornado appears to have curved quickly to the northeast, taking a few roof panels off a nearby outbuilding. Now approaching the bend in the road of W CR 50 S, the tornado appears to have intensified sharply with intense destruction and uprooting of trees, resulting in a clear convergent pattern. Nearby buildings appear to have avoided significant damage. On yet another sharp jaunt to the north, now headed to a farmstead, the tornado continued to destroy trees but also destroyed two barns, removed portions of roof off three other outbuildings, and completely destroyed a grain bin. Debris was gathered at the base of a nearby tree line. Aloft, a few large branches appear to have been snapped. Beyond this, trees are untouched suggesting the tornado lifted.

Video and storm chaser report confirm a tornado. This tornado crossed I-39 southwest of Lee and then tracked northeast, ending in a field in the vicinity of Tower Road north of Hermann Road. No known damage was caused by this tornado.

A brief tornado touched down near the Tippecanoe River causing tree and home damage to several properties along Tippecanoe Ranch Road and Horshoe Bend Road, crossing the Tippecanoe River 2 to 3 times. Two roofs showed significant damage. The tornado then made an easterly turn, impacting two homes along US 421 before impacting a hog farm near County Road 500N causing roof damage. Signs of ground circulation was noted in the fields near the farm. The tornado then dissipated in an open filed southwest of 550N.

This tornado tracked east-northeastward between Paxton and Loda, destroying a couple of outbuildings, peeling shingles off of a house, blowing a couple of semi-trailers over on Interstate 57, and damaging a few trees along its slightly under 7-mile-long track.

The third tornado, an EF-1, from the Dekalb/Daviess County supercell began just southeast of Jameson near Highway 13, destroying a pole barn along 235th Street. The tornado tracked northeast and caused extensive damage to several trees on a property near 250th and Route P. The path continued to the east-northeast, causing tree damage before ending just before the Grundy County line between Jameson and Trenton. The timing of this tornado was tied to spotter reports, as a second supercell traversed the same area about 30 minutes later.  However, spotter reports clearly tied this to the leading supercell.

The second tornado of the Dekalb/Daviess County supercell began north of Lake Viking just east of Interstate 35.  It damaged trees and a manufactured home along Lilac Avenue.  The tornado traveled to the east-northeast and crossed Route DD.  It continued across the Grand River and caused tree damage on the south side of Jameson before dissipating.  This tornado was timed to spotter reports in the area, since two supercells essentially traveled the same path.
A brief EF-0 tornado occurred near the intersection of Route E and 8th Street north of Laredo, causing some minor tree damage.

A tornado began near Farm Road 1078, just to the northwest of Butterfield. NWS ground surveys concluded that the tornado path tracked to the east across Highway 37. A couple of old wooden power poles snapped or were brought down along Highway 37. Several uprooted trees and large branches snapped along the path. Sentinel-2 satellite data analysis revealed that the tornado continued to the northeast, crossing State Highway U, producing an intermittent path of tree damage about 6.6 miles long. Satellite data revealed the tornado was 350 yards at its widest point with estimated max winds of 85 mph.

A rapidly developing supercell thunderstorm produced a tornado north of Ravanna, MO, on the afternoon of 10 June. The storm caused extensive damage to a garage and barn near the intersection of Route M and Route W east of Mercer.  The tornado crossed Bobcat Street to the northeast. Owing to inaccessibility to property to the northeast, relied on spotter reports to confirm that the track continued northeastward to Route M east of Route W southwest of Cleopatra, where extensive tree damage was observed. No damage indicators were found closer to the town of Cleopatra.

The National Weather Service storm survey determined that an EF-1 tornado with peak winds of 90mph touched down 1 mile east southeast of Fidelity. The tornado lifted and rolled a secured carport before moving to the east northeast. Multiple trees were were uprooted or snapped off between 4 and 6 feet up along an intermittent path to a home along County Road 120. There were multiple 2 to 3 foot in diameter trees downed in a convergent pattern, with a home suffering significant roof and structural damage from the fallen tree. In addition, a truck was crushed under the a tree before the tornado lifted just east of the home in an open field.

Tornado damage was first noted near the intersection of Cider Mill Road and Georgetown Road, with some trees snapped and uprooted. As the tornado travelled southeast, it ripped off a metal roof of a business on State Route 9 and lofted pieces of the metal sheet 800ft into neighboring properties and into the trees. Several trees in this location were also snapped half way up the base or uprooted. Additional damage was noted, again to trees along Steward Rd and Hunt Road. Here, trees were uprooted and snapped, bringing down a power pole. A house also had some shingles removed and three large pines uprooted. A definitive path continued to the south and east with additional damage noted along Depot Road, State Route 45, Salem Grange Road, Lisbon Road and just south of State route 558. All of this damage was to trees. The tornado then lifted just west of State Route 11, near Lower Elkton Road, where damage became much more sporadic and more indicative of straight-line winds. 

The National Weather Service would like to thank Columbiana County Emergency Management for assistance on this survey.

A brief tornado touched down along Highway 97 to the south of Capps Creek. The intermittent tornado path tracked to the east-northeast before lifting just west of Highway 37, between Monett and Purdy. Several uprooted trees and large branches snapped along the path. Walls collapsed on two farm outbuildings, with sheet metal tossed over 300 yards.

A second supercell in Mercer County produced a brief EF-0 tornado near U.S. Highway 65 north of Princeton on 10 June, continuing to the northeast across Finch Avenue before lifting near Muddy Creek. The tornado produced tree damage and bent over power poles on Finch Avenue.

The tornado touched down about 5 miles southwest of Bement, near the intersection of County Rd 600 and N 500 East Rd where it damaged two large trees. The tornado progressed through open fields just south of State Hwy 105, where a drone captured the rotational marks in the corn fields. The tornado removed the roof of a grain storage building and snapped two power poles where Hwy 105 turns north toward Bement. A camper was flipped over and destroyed along N 1000 East Rd, then the tornado moved northeast and cause damage to a grain bin, a couple of outbuildings and several trees along E 900 North Rd before it dissipated before reaching the county line.

The tornado touched down about 2 miles west-northwest of Argenta
where it damaged an outbuilding and some trees. It progressed
east through Argenta where it snapped off several trees. The
tornado produced mainly tree damage as it moved east along Newburg
Rd before dissipating 3 miles south of Cisco.
Photos and reports from storm spotters indicate that a brief tornado occurred in a field south of E 6000S Road. No known damage was caused by this tornado.

A brief EF-0 tornado with winds to 80 mph touched down just on the west side of the Cal Sag Channel and tracked eastward across portions of Alsip. This tornado impacted areas roughly between W 120th Pl and W 121st St. Most of the damage consisted of uprooted or snapped trees, along with some downed power poles and lines. The total path length was approximately 2.5 miles long, with a max width of 175 yards.

This tornado began in a field southwest of E 2600 N Road and N 190 East Road. It tracked into Long Point, where some tree damage was noted before continuing northeast with sporadic damage near Ancona and Reading Township. The tornado intensified as it crossed east of N 500 East Road, where it blew a grain bin off its foundation and dragged it along the ground for approximately 700 yards. The tornado reached its peak intensity on the southeast side of Streator near the Livingston-La Salle county line. Here, several houses along Sunbury Drive were heavily damaged. At one residence, only the inner-most walls were left standing, with debris tossed southward, upstream against the tornado path. Damage in this area was consistent with EF-3 winds around 145 mph. The tornado continued northeast before turning nearly due north, causing damage consistent with EF-2 caliber winds to several residences along E 19th Road. The tornado appears to have lifted northeast of Streator near N 1475th Road.

This tornado destroyed an outbuilding at a farmstead about 2.5 miles northeast of Wellington. It also downed a few power poles and left a clear, narrow damage path through crops in a field to the east of N 2700 East Road and north of E 500 North Road before dissipating shortly thereafter.

A National Weather Service Cleveland storm survey determined that a brief tornado touched down in central Crawford County near Leimbach Road at approximately 4:29 PM EDT. The tornado touched down west of Leimbach Road and north of Double Hill Road, then moved generally east-southeast.

Damage consisted primarily of snapped and uprooted trees. Several trees were snapped near the point of touchdown, and a falling tree clipped and damaged a well-constructed detached garage. As the tornado crossed Leimbach Road, several large hardwood trees were uprooted. The fallen trees were oriented toward the northeast, consistent with the localized tornadic wind field despite the tornado's overall east-southeast movement.

Based on the observed damage, maximum wind speeds were estimated at 93 mph, yielding an EF-1 tornado rating. The tornado had an estimated maximum width of 50 yards and produced a short, intermittent damage path before dissipating.

A National Weather Service Cleveland storm survey determined that a brief EF-1 tornado touched down in central Crawford County at approximately 4:28 PM EDT, south of Dibble Hill Road and east of Theuret Hill Road, and tracked southeast.
