The tornado snapped several large tree limbs near the point of touchdown before crossing Stoltz Road, where several large trees were uprooted and fell onto a detached garage. A power pole snapped and fell toward the northwest even as the tornado moved southeast. Leaves and hay debris were scattered and pasted across the east side of a barn and nearby structures, indicating rotational winds. Additional trees were snapped and uprooted south of the property and within a tree line to the east.

Based on the damage, maximum winds were estimated at 90 mph, yielding an EF-1 rating. The tornado had an estimated maximum width of 75 yards.

The National Weather Service Cleveland thanks the Crawford County EMA for its assistance during the storm survey.
Short-lived QLCS tornado resulted in damage to two residential properties along Paulen Road.

Concentrated damage was first noted by Darlington Road and Clayton Road, which is coincident with a tightening couplet on the radar. Damage in this location was mainly to trees, with large branches snapped and one tree uprooted. Damage then continued along Clayton road and in the neighborhood just south of Clayton Road. Some siding was ripped off of a home on George St and trees were snapped off at varying levels in a southeastward direction. A garage was smashed after a portion of a pine tree was sheared off at its top. Tree damage was noted until around 27th street, when the tornado appears to have lifted and the radar signature weakens.

Several storm chaser videos confirm a brief tornado began in a field between N 975 East and N 1100 East roads. Videos clearly show this tornado crossed E 3200 North Road and dissipated in a field just south of the LaSalle-Livingston county line. No known damage is associated with this tornado, leading to an EF-U designation.

With the guidance of Jefferson County EMA, a survey team from NWS Pittsburgh evaluated damage from Sunday's storms in Jefferson County, PA. The team has confirmed that the damage observed was the result of a tornado.

Damage was first seen in a wooded area bounded by Nickles Road and London Road, mainly in the form of sporadic snapped limbs.

As the storm emerged from the wooded area, it snapped softwood trees at a farmstead near Burns and Anita Oliveburg Road. 

The tornado weakened briefly as it progressed eastward, with intermittent damage to limbs along Anita Oliveburg Road and Blocks Rd, including one on a shed.

After crossing to Knox Dale Road, the tornadic circulation strengthened and grew in size, and damage became considerably more consistent and notable. Beginning here and continuing northeast toward Route 310, large swaths of healthy and sturdy hardwood and softwood trees were snapped and uprooted, most notably near Team Road and along an adjacent hillside. On this hillside was the most significant damage, where almost no tree was left intact. Despite the increase in intensity, damage to adjacent structures appeared limited, suggesting the gradient in wind speed across the tornadic circulation was sharp.

**NEW** Based on drone video and photography, wind speed along the segment of the path from Knox Dale Road along Team Road was estimated to be up to 115 mph. This tornado has been upgraded to EF2 strength.*** 

After descending the hill along Route 310 toward Shane Dr, the circulation weakened only slightly, and damage continued, consisting of snapped and uprooted trees. Also in this area, a home lost its carport and suffered light damage to siding and roof material. Here wind was most consistent with 90-100 mph speed.

***NEW***Damage to a barn and trees along Graffius Ave Ext was brought to the survey team's attention on Tuesday, enabling the survey team to extend the prior path over the hillside adjacent to Shane Dr.***

The most significant observed damage is consistent with EF2 wind speed (max wind 115 mph). 

No tornadic damage was reported elsewhere across Jefferson County.  Additional extensive searches for damage were conducted in the Ringgold area, and near Corsica, to no avail.

As of this update, the tornado's path is updated to 3.8 miles long, with a maximum width of 300 yd.

NWS Pittsburgh is grateful for the assistance of Jefferson County EMA, local township fire department personnel, and the public for their damage reports and aerial imagery that facilitated the completion of this survey.

A storm survey team from The National Weather Service office in State College confirmed an EF-1 tornado near Kirkwood in Lancaster County. Maximum winds of 90-100 mph snapped several tree trunks and large limbs. The damage began on Wesley Rd between Puseyville Rd and Noble Rd in Little Britain Township at approximately 9:32 PM EDT on Sunday, Jun 14. Over the next 5 minutes, the tornado continued into Colerain Township, producing sporadic damage including damage to trees on Noble Rd near White Rock Rd and damage to power poles on Kirkwood Pike near Morrison Mill Rd.

The tornado touched down about 3 miles northwest of Mount Pulaski
where it did some minor tree damage. The tornado intensified as it
progressed east along 900 St, where it did extensive tree damage for
about a half mile, damaging numerous trees. The tornado angled
southeast and crossed Hwy 54 producing more tree damage. The tornado
produced mainly tree damage for the remainder of its time on the
ground, dissipating about 3 miles north of Forsyth.

Cell that produced the tornado northwestward over Salem continued to track southeastward toward Negley OH with a much weaker presentation on radar then it had prior. Just before the storm reached the border, another tightening of the couplet was noted coincident with a swath of damage along and south of  Darlington/Cannelton Road, with several trees downed along the Youngstown & Southern Railroad tracks and on a property just across the PA line into Beaver County. At this location, an awning of a garage was ripped off and flipped over the garage from south to north as trees were snapped and uprooted through the property. This would be where the tornado would be it's strongest before beginning to weaken as it moved to the south and west. Some tree damage was noted just south of Cannelton Road before Watts Mills Road but no additional damage was noted east of there. Pending additional aerial surveys, the track could be extended but the radar not long after this location a storm developing ahead of this one most likely interacted with a disturbed tornadogenesis.
This tornado tracked across the south side of Watseka before ending near the intersection of US Route 24 and IL State Route 1. Damage along the tornado's path was largely confined to trees.

Damage began just west of Stone Spring House Road in a wooded area, where large tree branches were broken.  It crossed to an area south of Breedtown Road, with a continuing swath of fallen trees.

A delayed report of a home with roof damage south of the Titusville Airport runway was conveyed to NWS Pittsburgh by local Fire Department personnel. This location is coincident with radar indication of very strong, compact rotation off of the Pleasantville radar, suggesting the tornadic circulation was ongoing.

Additional damage near Dempseytown Greshem Rd, Fairview Rd and Barker Rd also was brought to the attention of NWS Pittsburgh, also near the continuing radar-indicated compact vortex, likely the result of the dissipating tornado.

The tornado appears to have weakened rapidly thereafter.

A broad (almost 3.0 miles in width) swath of damage to trees from Wilson Mills to Bradleytown/Plum Corner to Sunville to Wallaceville appears to be caused by a strong surge of wind on the southern flank of a mesovortex that crossed this region at the same time that the tornado to the north was beginning to form.

NWS Pittsburgh appreciates the large number of photos and reports provided by residents in the affected areas that have enabled us to identify damage swaths in northern Venango County more completely.

Tornado began west of a farm in an open field and moved east southeast through the northern portion of Belleville. Numerous trees were snapped and uprooted. Peeled shingles and siding as well as damage to soffit and guttering on several homes. A garage one on home fell in after its roof was lifted. A garage on another home was breached at the garage door and the structure failed, peeling downwind and taking a large portion of the dwelling's roof decking. The tornado continued east southeast over a farm field damaging corn and a long water sprinkler. The end of the path east of County Road D featured additional trees snapped and uprooted before lifting in the Brooklyn Wildlife Area.

The tornado developed 4 miles north of Mattoon and tracked southeast, damaging trees, homes, and electrical transmission lines as it crossed US Highway 45. It intensified as it reached County Rd 700E, uprooting large hardwood trees and lifting the roof off a single family residence. It continued east-southeast from there, crossing Interstate 57 where it flipped a semi, resulting in one injury. It then heavily damaged a few farm outbuildings and trees on the western outskirts of Charleston. It continued eastward through the north side of Charleston, causing damage at the fairgrounds, a few outbuildings, and trees throughout town before lifting 2 miles east of Charleston along Illinois 16.

NWS ground survey confirmed an EF-1 tornado with maximum sustained winds of 105 mph tracked from Treasure Isle in southeast St. Tammany Parish to rural parts of southwest Hancock County, north of Pearlington. The tornado began near or before moving into Treasure Isle where it flipped a large boat on its side. Additional visible damage to homes and lofting of outdoor fixtures was noted as the tornado moved into Martin Drive. The tornado reached EF-1 intensity near Bluegill Drive where it removed shingles off of homes, snapped a few trees, and collapsed garage door structures and blew out a wall or two as a result in two different homes. A defined damage path was observed on LA Hwy 433 and then crossed into inaccesible marsh areas. A weak tornado debris signature was evident on KHDC and is the basis for connecting this damage to Avery Estates. The tornado continued northeast into Avery Estates where minor metal roof damage and tree damage was noted on Avery Drive and Smokey Hollow Drive. The tornado evidently strengthened and grew in size to around 300 yards in width as it moved just south of the northern part of Avery Drive and into US Hwy 190 where numerous trees were uprooted or snapped. Several outbuildings were damaged and tension cables on a cell tower were snapped. It's possible the tornado slowed in this area as it pivoted and turned more to the east per KHDC radar imagery. Along US Hwy 190 a manufactured home had most of its roof removed and it was shifted significantly off its foundation. The tornado then moved into Pearl River Basin, inaccessible to ground survey. The tornado evidently maintained strength or even strengthened further over this area, evidenced by the deepening of a tornado debris signature lofted over 5000 feet. Tree damage was found by ground survey team on rural roads of southwest Hancock County as the tornado began to weaken and lift back to the northeast. The tornado is estimated to have lifted near or after Point Road prior to reaching MS Hwy 607.
A trained spotter reported a brief tornado touchdown near Tower Hill. No damage was reported.

A tornado briefly touched down just west of Coppinville Junior High School. The tornado damaged an awning on the westernmost building of the school and tossed some debris around the lawn. The tornado then crossed a wooded area spapping some branches before lifting northwest of Thornbird Loop. The track was flown by drone and video footage also captured the tornado. Damage was minor, consistent with EF0 strength with maximumwind estimated to be 70 mph.

NWS Pittsburgh has confirmed a brief tornado southeast of Derry, PA from a storm on July 18, 2026.

Sporadic damage primarily to trees was noted along a path beginning near Carey Ln and continuing southeast across Matson Rd through heavily wooded areas.  A review of aerial photography has helped identify impacted areas inaccessible by foot.

At its peak, damage appears consistent with wind of up to 70 mph.

Beyond this point, no damage was evident.  However, the path, magnitude and width of the tornado is subject to change pending additional reported damage coming to light.

A personal video was received that showed damage just to the west/southwest of property along Oldson Road in far southeast Bourbon County. The video clearly depicts lofted debris, with a small circulation moving across the field. A field survey was unable to reach the suspected minor tree damage. 

A big thanks to NWS Jackson, KYEM, and Bourbon County Emergency Management who helped up with this survey and tracking this video down.

This tornado formed near the intersection of S 500 W and W 1075 S roads in Washington Township. It tracked northeastward through rural portions of central Newton County for several miles before ending near Curtis Creek Country Club in Newton Township in western Jasper County, west of Rensselaer. Along its over 15-mile-long path, the tornado damaged or destroyed multiple farm outbuildings, downed several trees and tree limbs, downed a few power poles, and destroyed a grain bin.

A National Weather Service Cleveland storm survey determined that a brief EF-0 tornado touched down on the west side of Conneautville, Pennsylvania, at about 4:10 PM EDT on Sunday, June 14, 2026.

The tornado left a path of damage, uprooting several trees and snapping large limbs along Mulberry Lane and Mulberry Street. The circulation then moved east across Mulberry Street, causing additional tree damage before dissipating shortly thereafter. Additionally, several trees were uprooted and snapped along State Highway 198.

Based on the observed damage, the tornado's maximum winds were estimated at 85 mph, yielding an EF-0 rating. The tornado was 100 yards wide. It was brief and produced a relatively short damage path before evolving into straight-line thunderstorm winds.

Although the tornadic circulation ended, strong straight-line winds persisted south of the tornado path. These winds caused additional damage, including several trees downed across the railroad tracks near Main Street and Smith Avenue. Maximum straight-line wind speeds reached 80 mph.

A storm survey team from The National Weather Service office in State College confirmed microburst damage in Brogue, York County. The most concentrated damage occurred along Forry Road in Chanceford Township where 80-90 mph estimated maximum winds knocked down or snapped 10 trees and caused shingle damage to one home. One tree landed on a car. We thank York County Emergency Management and local homeowners for their assistance with this survey.

The tornado touched down east of US 231 with the first area of damage occurring along County Road 250 East with significant damage to a mobile home. The tornado then moved along 600S with damage noted to two groves of trees between 425E and 550E. The tornado also impacted two homes and destroyed one barn in that area. The tornado then moved mostly through farm fields in eastern Putnam county with the tornado likely skipping at times before it ended just on the Morgan county side.

The tornado began southwest of the intersection of Saint Joe Highway and Oneida Road and damaged mostly trees along its path. Near the Oneida Township Hall, a storage outbuilding was completely destroyed. Some minor additional property damage was noted along the path, mainly due to fallen trees. The tornado lifted in a field just east of St Johns Chase Road and south of W Eaton Highway.
Brief rope tornado along Co Hwy 39 north of I-90. Confirmed by law enforcement and video via storm chaser.

The tornado began in Vigo County south of Riley impacting mostly trees along East Dallas Drive before crossing into Clay county and doing the most significant damage of the path along 2 residences on County Road 200S. Both homes had their roofs completely lifted and blown away with a garage also destroyed. Several outbuildings were also destroyed or damaged along with tree damage across the properties. There was additional tree and barn damage further east along 200S with another concentrated area of damage along a home along 425W. This home had a 100 year old brick barn partially destroyed along with tree damage on the property. An abandoned home next door also experienced damage but it was difficult to determine what damage was new. As the tornado continued to the east it mostly impacted a grove of trees with another home impacted on County Road 200S west of 250W. The tornado then lifted just to the west of 250W.
updated track based on new information

An EF1 tornado touched down on the east bank of the MS River and moved northeast to the University of New Orleans. Damage across the city was mostly tree damage and minor building damage. Additional analysis, points and information will be added later. Additional changes are possible.

The first evidence of tornado damage occurred along Gobblers Knob Road, where some trees were damaged. Additional damage was found on Seeley Road, where large tree limbs were knocked down. The tornado moved east, producing more tree damage along Johnson Fork Road. The tornado strengthened as it moved into Drewersburg, producing more significant tree damage along Welsh Drive and Drewersburg Road. One single family home along Welsh Road had its roof completely lifted off with collapse of some exterior walls. Winds that produced this damage were estimated to be around 125 mph, which corresponds to an EF-2 rating on the Enhanced Fujita Scale. A roof was also lifted off a home on Drewersburg Road. 

The tornado curved southeast as it moved onto State Line Road, blowing some large tree limbs down. The tornado weakened to EF-0 intensity as it moved into Butler County, Ohio. A few large tree limbs were knocked down on Schradin Road, and this is believed to be the end of the tornado. 

The National Weather Service would like to thank the Franklin County, Indiana Emergency Management Agency and the Butler County, Ohio Emergency Agency for their assistance and support with this damage survey.

A National Weather Service Cleveland storm survey determined that an EF-1 tornado touched down at approximately 4:51 PM EDT on Sunday, June 14, 2026, along Lippert Road, just east of the intersection with Mallory Road in Crawford County.

The tornado tracked east along Lippert Road, causing significant damage to one residence, including roof damage, the loss of an attached porch, damage to four vehicles, displacement of an RV approximately 50 feet, and damage to a garage roof. An additional six homes sustained minor damage, including damage to roofs, siding, and windows.

As the tornado continued east, numerous trees were blown down, blocking driveways and roadways. Several large limbs snapped and fell onto a barn and a nearby home. The tornado gradually weakened and dissipated northwest of the intersection of Lippert Road and Vincent Road.

Based on the observed damage, maximum winds were estimated at 90 mph, resulting in an EF-1 rating. The tornado had an estimated maximum width of 50 yards.

The National Weather Service Cleveland appreciates the assistance provided for this storm survey and thanks Crawford County EMA for their support in documenting the damage.
A NWS survey team concluded an EF-0 tornado produced damage to trees, several homes, and several electrical wooden poles in the McCord area of Houma. Time estimated by radar.

A National Weather Service ground survey determined that an EF-1 tornado with estimated peak winds of 95 mph occurred a mile southwest of Mount Zion in Douglas County, lasting approximately 2 minutes and traveling a half mile. The tornado produced a 75 yard wide path of tree damage consisting of snapped trunks, uprooted trees, and large branches thrown around. Track extensions are still possible with additional satellite data analysis.

A tornado briefly touched down just west of Coppinville Junior High School. The tornado damaged an awning on the westernmost building of the school and tossed some debris around the lawn. The tornado then crossed a wooded area spapping some branches before lifting northwest of Thornbird Loop. The track was flown by drone and video footage also captured the tornado. Damage was minor, consistent with EF0 strength with maximumwind estimated to be 70 mph.

A tornado touched down in an open field and snapped multiple trees along N 1050th St southwest of Rose Hill. The tornado probably dissipated in the trees near Lick Creek after being on the ground for about 2  minutes.

A tornado touched down approximately 4 to 5 miles southwest of Maddock and tracked southeast where it hit a shelterbelt and barns doing EF-0 damage. The track is based on Sentinel satellite analysis showing scarring associated with the tornado tracking to the southeast towards where the damage to the trees and barns were filmed. Width is approximated from scarring visible on Sentinel satellite with the maximum width occurring to the southwest of Legreid Lake early on in the lifecycle.

NWS Pittsburgh has confirmed a brief tornado southeast of Derry, PA from a storm on July 18, 2026.

Sporadic damage primarily to trees was noted along a path beginning near Carey Ln and continuing southeast across Matson Rd through heavily wooded areas.  A review of aerial photography has helped identify impacted areas inaccessible by foot.

At its peak, damage appears consistent with wind of up to 70 mph.

Beyond this point, no damage was evident.  However, the path, magnitude and width of the tornado is subject to change pending additional reported damage coming to light.

The first evidence of tornadic damage occurred on Union Hill Road in Pike County about six tenths of a mile north of Appalachian Highway where a few hardwood trees were snapped and multiple limbs were broken off trees. The tornado then moved through a heavily forested area towards the intersection of Lansing Road and Chenoweth Fork Road where more tree damage was noted. Tree damage continued in a concentrated path to the east northeast along Chenoweth Fork Road before crossing Appalachian Highway and causing a fair amount of tree damage at a rest station on Meads Road. The damage noted in the first third of the tornado’s path consisted of broken branches, snapped trunks, and uprooting of mature trees. This is consistent with EF0 and EF1 damage. 

After the damage occurred at the Meads Road rest station, the tornado continued east through a forest with a large hillside that was not reachable by ground survey. This coincided with the first evidence of a Tornadic Debris Signature on the Wilmington, OH radar. When the tornado came down the ridgeline just west of Elm Grove, the most significant damage indicators were noted. An entire section of hardwood forest, about 200-250 yards wide, was blown down. Drone photography and ground survey confirms all hardwood trees in this location were snapped with none left standing. The estimate for this type of tree damage is around 115 mph, which is consistent with low end EF2 damage.  

Some higher-end EF1 damage was observed as the tornado moved northeast off the hillside into Elm Grove where complete collapse of out buildings and barns, 70% removal of a roof off a house, and snapping of large power transmission lines occurred. After Elm Grove, the tornado turned southeast causing additional damage near the intersection of SR 772 and Appalachian Highway. The final evidence of tree damage was located on Sun Fish Creek Road about a half mile south of Tennyson Road. 

The National Weather Service would like to thank The Pike County Ohio Emergency Management Agency and the Ohio Emergency Agency for their assistance and support with this damage survey.

An EF-1 tornado touched down 2 miles north of Lynnville, crossed Spurgeon Road, and lifted 2.5 miles northeast of Lynville along Gore Road. Several power poles were leaning and a few trees experienced some broken large branches. Thank you to Warrick County EMA for their assistance with this survey.

The tornado first touched down just northwest of the intersection of King Bee Rd and Ten Mile Church Rd. The tornado uprooted trees at a residence at Spiers Rd and King Bee Rd. The tornado intensified and likely reached its maximum intensity as it moved northeast toward Flint Creek Road. Numerous trees were snapped and uprooted. In addition, the roof was torn off of a residence and a mobile home, and roof damage was observed to several sheds and outside storage buildings. The tornado continued northeast and weakened as it crossed John Willis Rd. The tornado briefly intensified again to EF-1 strength as it crossed Highway 26 where several trees were uprooted and snapped. The tornado weakened and lifted as it crossed Big Four Rd north of Highway 26.

Review of Sentinel 2 and Planet high resolution satellite imagery revealed the tornado path to have started earlier along Ten Mile Church Road where scattered tree damage became apparent in a focused corridor. To the south, scattered trees were damaged in association with the storms RFD. The maximum tornado width has also been adjusted to approximately 375 yards.

NWS Pittsburgh has confirmed a brief tornado southeast of Derry, PA from a storm on July 18, 2026.

Sporadic damage primarily to trees was noted along a path beginning near Carey Ln and continuing southeast across Matson Rd through heavily wooded areas.  A review of aerial photography has helped identify impacted areas inaccessible by foot.

At its peak, damage appears consistent with wind of up to 70 mph.

Beyond this point, no damage was evident.  However, the path, magnitude and width of the tornado is subject to change pending additional reported damage coming to light.

The first evidence of tornadic damage was observed at a single family residence off of Henry Rd, where a hardwood tree was snapped and fell onto the roof of the home. Additionally, the field adjacent to the home had some flattened corn stalks, with minor tree damage also observed across the street. More flattened corn stalk was found in a field near the intersection of Henry Rd and State Highway 729. 

The most significant damage came along Larrick Rd, with several properties observing tree damage. One property in particular had six trees that were either uprooted or snapped at the base. Wind speeds in this area were likely near 75 MPH, which corresponds to EF-0 strength on the Enhanced Fujita Scale. 

The last observed damage came on Larrick Rd where a tree was uprooted and additional corn stalk was partially flattened. No other visible evidence was observed to the south and east of this property. 

The National Weather Service would like to thank the Clinton County Emergency Management Agency for their assistance with this storm damage survey.

The National Weather Service has confirmed an EF1 tornado in Carroll, Gallatin, Owen, and Grant counties in Kentucky. This tornado occurred during the afternoon of July 21, 2026.

The first evidence of the tornado was along Kentucky State Route 47 near and northwest of Interstate 71 in Carroll County, where some large branches and a couple trees were downed. Much more significant damage occurred between the Gallatin County Airport and Eagle Creek, including State Route 467. Significant tree damage was noted here, including a majority of the trees along the Eagle Creek bottomland with their trunks snapped. This is believed to be one of the locations where the tornado was near peak intensity, with maximum winds of around 110 MPH. Drone footage provided by the Gallatin County Sheriff's Office confirmed the scope of the tree damage at this location. Additional stands of snapped trees were observed near New Liberty Sparta Road.

As the tornado moved into Owen County, a property on State Route 35 near US Route 127 sustained significant damage to numerous outbuildings. On Stewart Ridge Road, one residence was destroyed, with wood posts on a concrete slab snapped off. An injury occurred at this location when a large RV was rolled by the tornado. An old tobacco barn near this location was destroyed, and several snapped trees were also observed in the vicinity.

On Golden Circle Road and Jonesville Road, numerous trees were downed, and roof damage was observed on several outbuildings. One home on Jonesville Road had its roof lifted. Another outbuilding was destroyed at a property on Agee Road, with significant damage to trees along the hillside near this location. Drone footage provided by Owen County Search and Rescue provided significant help for determining the location of damage in this area.

The tornado weakened somewhat as it approached State Route 22, with just a few trees damaged. However, a more concentrated area of downed trees was noted near the bridge on Cross Roads Drive and Lusby Mill Road, as the tornado crossed from Owen County into Grant County. One house near this bridge had significant roof damage. The last observed damage was at a property north of Keefer Road. At this property, three outbuildings were mostly or completely destroyed, and the house lost a significant portion of its roof. The brick garage of the house was shifted very slightly on its slab foundation, with cracks in some of the bricks noted. Debris from this location was carried into the tree line to the east. This location is also a place where the tornado was near peak intensity, with maximum winds of around 110 MPH. The tornado weakened as it moved east, with occasional additional damage noted north of Keefer Road, on US Route 27, and on Fork Lick Road.

The National Weather Service would like to thank the emergency management agencies in Carroll, Gallatin, Owen, and Grant counties, along with Kentucky Emergency Management Area 6, for their assistance in this damage survey.

A National Weather Service ground survey determined that an EF-0 tornado with estimated peak winds of 80 mph occurred 2 miles north of Mountain Dale, or 4 miles north of Seymour. Both video of the tornado and the ground survey revealed an intermittent 75 yard wide path of mostly tree damage, lasting for 6 minutes and traveling one and a half miles. The most substantial damage was a tin roof blown off a barn. Track extensions are still possible with satellite data analysis.

An NWS Storm Survey concluded than a long track, EF-2 tornado touched down in far eastern Grayson County, right along Nolin River Lake in the Wax, KY area. The worst of the accessible damage was noted here towards the beginning of the track, where winds of 115 mph did significant damage to some homes and outbuildings along Nolin River Lake. One injury was reported in this area where a man sustained a head injury from the tornado. 

The tornado maintained high-end EF-1 strength throughout much of the rest of its path through Hart County. This high end EF-1 damage was most widespread and pronounced from the town of Rowletts and southeast along Red Buck Estes Road. Most trees and structures had some sort of damage in these areas and this is likely where the tornado was at its peak width. The tornado continued southeast along Lonoke Road into the small town of Uno, KY, where it finally lifted before crossing into Metcalfe County, KY. In total, the path was over 20 miles long and this tornado was on the ground continuously for 41 minutes!

NWS Louisville would like to express gratitude to Kentucky Emergency Management, Grayson County Emergency Management, and Hart County Emergency management for their timely reports of the damage and their help with the survey process.

Survey damage suggests a tornado began west of North Humpty Dumpty Road south of Patricksburg, IN just before 7:00 PM local time, and continued eastward for 3 minutes before lifting near North Byerly Road. This tornado caused sporadic tree damage mostly consisting of large tree limbs and a few small tree trunks.

The tornado touched down about 1.5 miles west of Pawnee Junction near the I-55 exit, then traveled east across I-55 affecting Commanche Village and the town of Pawnee before dissipating 0.75 miles southeast of Pawnee. During its time on the ground it produced mainly EF0 tree damage, along with minor damage to home soffits and roofs. No injuries were reported. during its 5.7 mile path.

At least two storm chaser videos show this brief tornado touch down east of Illinois Route 18/North 1200 E Road just north of the LaSalle-Livingston county line near a wind farm. No known damage is associated with this tornado, leading to an EF-U designation.

On the evening of June 16, the National Weather Service received numerous reports of a supercell with a rotating wall cloud. Cass County Emergency Management and storm chasers maintained watch over the storm. Two storm chasers on X provided photo and video evidence of brief touchdown in this area. Emergency management, farther south at this time, also indicated a possible touchdown. The tornado occurred over an open field with no damage indicators. As a result, an EF-U (unknown) tornado has been recorded.

A NWS survey team concluded that an EF-1 tornado tracked from the corner of Afton St and Richmond Ave towards Dixie Ave in Houma. A truck was tossed 30 feet and sustained significant damage. Multiple snapped and uprooted trees were observed.  Several homes sustained a partial loss of their roofs. One home had a collapsed carport. Time estimated by radar.

An EF1 Tornado hit Rock Stream, NY, crossed Seneca Lake and hit lakeshore residence south of Hector, NY during late morning on June 18, 2026. Though there was pockets of minor tree damage from the storm itself, tornadic damage started around Reading Road at 1045 AM. This tornado strengthened to as much as 90 mph from Old Lake Road to State Route 14, as rotation tightened with the storm quickly moving at 50 mph from higher elevations into the Seneca Lake basin. Numerous trees were uprooted in a convergent chaotic fashion, and around 40 vineyard posts were snapped. Twigs and branches were impaled into the ground as missiles in portions of the vineyard, and shingles were found more than a quarter mile from their source. A garage outbuilding collapsed, with some metal roof peelback and siding damage also noted on the residence with small branches squeezing into gaps. After crossing State Route 14 with a continued corridor of uprooted trees, the tornado crossed Seneca Lake around 1050 AM. Significant damage was observed near the lake at the end of Wickham Rd. A large tree branch was impaled into a house and several trees and numerous large branches were downed.

A NWS survey team concluded an EF-1 tornado tracked from Evelyn Ave towards Woodhaven Dr and Roberta Grove Blvd.  Several businesses in the Lynn Park Shopping Center (at the corner of Prospect Ave and Grand Caillou Rd) sustained damage to almost every window and had partially collapsed interior walls and their roof. HVAC equipment on the roof was thrown northward onto the ground from these businesses. 4 homes had partial to significant roof loss.  One home had an exterior wall collapsed.  Several carports were significantly damaged.

An EF-0 tornado briefly touched down 3.4 miles west of Cortland in Cortland County NY around 11:32 AM, moving east-northeast at 50 mph. Tree damage along the route was the most common type of damage, with a swath of tree damage showing a convergent pattern, which is indication of a brief tornado touching down. Going east along Route 222, and along residential streets south of Route 222, multiple trees fell in the east-northeast direction, with a few falling due north. Where convergent damage was evident was just north of the Cortland County Airport, with a few trees falling in the southwest direction. Among the damage, some of the most extensive was mainly large uprooted trees and large snapped trees. Going further east-northeast, further scattered tree damage was observed, but did not show a convergent pattern. This indicated that the brief tornado dissipated heading into town, and was residual thunderstorm wind damage.

A NWS survey team concluded that an EF-1 tornado tracked northeast across Hancock and Harrison counties. Tree damage was widespread along the track including several large trees uprooted and snapped. Minor damage was done to several properties. Additional revisions via high resolution satellite analysis concluded the tornado began west of Standard Dedeaux Rd, north of Rock Hill Dedeaux Rd where it quickly strengthened into an EF-1 tornado and reached its peak width of 275 yards wide. The tornado then evidently weakened and the damage path become more intermittent until it reached the Wolf River where another swath of trees was rated low-end EF-1. The tornado damage path became intermittent once more after crossing the intersection of Cemetery and Steel Bridge Rd. The tornado then evidently reached its third peak as an EF-1 tornado as it crossed Cemetery Rd and MS Hwy 53 where swaths of trees were damaged and uprooted. The tornado then rapidly dissipated as it continued northeast and it's estimated to have lifted prior to reaching Herman Ladner Rd.

At approximately 6:08 AM, a tornado developed east of Stanton,
Iowa, near 230th Street and Q Avenue, and moved northeast. The
tornado produced tree damage on the west side of Viking Lake,
including large broken limbs and uprooted trees, with estimated
winds of 70 to 85 mph. The tornado then crossed to the east side
of Viking Lake, where it uprooted two trees, brought down
numerous large limbs, caused minor siding and roof damage to a
home near 230th Street and Raspberry Drive, and snapped
approximately 10 pine tree trunks near S Avenue and Aldersgate
Drive. Based on this damage, winds were estimated at 90 mph. The
tornado then continued northeast, collapsing the walls of an
outbuilding, snapping a tree trunk, and bringing down power lines
near U.S. Highway 24 and T Avenue. Based on this damage, peak
winds were estimated around 105 mph. The tornado then lofted
grain bins from over a mile away into the interchange of Highway
71 and Highway 34. The tornado dissipated at approximately
6:16 AM.

The tornado touched down about 1 mile southeast of Neoga, on the east side of I-57. It damaged a few farm outbuildings and trees along its path, which was less than 1 mile long, lifting just north of County Road 1000 N.

Weak tornado developed along Dover Hill Road to the southwest of Dover Hill. Tornado moved southeastward crossing SR 450 where a metal bard roof was peeled off and lofted 100 ft and convergence was noted in nearby snapped tree damage. Tornado continued southeast through inaccessible hilly terrain and diminished near Hickory Ridge Road to the north of Shoals.

The tornado began about 1 mile southeast of Bradbury near County Road 1350. It tracked northeast, damaging several trees and a couple of farm outbuildings. It turned east-northeastward and tracked just south of Cottonwood, causing more tree damage before lifting northwest of Diona near the county line.

A small satellite tornado developed to the south of the New Market Tornado, with damage first noted along Hurricane Rd. at 4:03 PM. At this point, trunks of large hardwood trees were partially snapped. The satellite tornado then traveled cyclonically within the circulation of the New Market Tornado, crossing the southern end of Backbone Mountain. Shortly before the satellite tornado merged with the New Market Tornado, it produced sporadic hard and soft wood tree damage along Upper Hurricane Road.

A tornado briefly touched down just west of Coppinville Junior High School. The tornado damaged an awning on the westernmost building of the school and tossed some debris around the lawn. The tornado then crossed a wooded area spapping some branches before lifting northwest of Thornbird Loop. The track was flown by drone and video footage also captured the tornado. Damage was minor, consistent with EF0 strength with maximumwind estimated to be 70 mph.

Path for landspout west of Albin WY on 7/7/26. This landspout formed underneath a developing cell that formed on a stationary convergence boundary in eastern Laramie County. This landspout tornado was very tall and reported by several observers with photos and video. Additionally, the circulation was evident on KCYS radar and lasted for approximately 12 minutes. Location determined from photos, video, and radar time-matching.

NWS Pittsburgh has confirmed a brief tornado southeast of Derry, PA from a storm on July 18, 2026.

Sporadic damage primarily to trees was noted along a path beginning near Carey Ln and continuing southeast across Matson Rd through heavily wooded areas.  A review of aerial photography has helped identify impacted areas inaccessible by foot.

At its peak, damage appears consistent with wind of up to 70 mph.

Beyond this point, no damage was evident.  However, the path, magnitude and width of the tornado is subject to change pending additional reported damage coming to light.

A brief tornado occurred on July 18, 2026 to the north of Latrobe.  An aerial damage survey suggests the tornado began near Red Cut Lodge Rd, and progressed southeast, crossing Route 981 before dissipating.

An earlier tornado LSR was issued confirming this tornado.  No damage to crops or trees was evident along Stewart Rd where the LSR was issued.

Damage with the tornado was consistent with wind gusts up to 75 mph, which leads to this tornado being rated EF0.  The path length, width and magnitude are all subject to change pending additional information received.

An EF-1 tornado occurred in northwestern Metcalfe County, near Knob Lick, during the late afternoon hours on July 21, 2026. The tornado first touched down just north of Glenn Finn Road at 5:19 PM CDT and continued south-southeast. The tornado produced EF-0 damage initially between Glenn Finn Road and Ratliff Mitchell Road. The tornado then strengthened as it crossed Ratliff Mitchell Road and produced winds over 100 mph and caused EF-1 damage, especially to a large barn near a residence on Pleasant Valley Church Road. Debris was lofted to the SSE across an empty field, and metal roof panels were found wrapped around trees nearly 1000 feet away along McCandless Coomer Road. 

The tornado continued southeastward nearly parallel to Pleasant Valley Church Road, eventually crossing it, and creating additional EF-1 tree damage. The tornado then lifted just north of Knob Lick at approximately 5:25 PM CDT, near the intersection of Pleasant Valley Church Road and Sulphur Well Knob Lick Road.

A short-lived EF-1 tornado developed in Monmouth Illinois and tracked southeast through town for 1.3 miles, with estimated maximum winds of 100 mph. Along the tornado path, structural damage was observed in the heart of Monmouth, with a few
buildings seeing roofing damage, many windows blown out, and part of their brick walls damaged. Some houses also saw loss of shingles. Otherwise, a lot of damage was observed to trees along a clear convergent path, with numerous snapped, uprooted, and a lot of trees with downed large branches throughout. Some of these large tree sections were downed on houses as well.

A brief EF1 tornado uniquely tracked across three states. This developed just inside Lee County, Iowa, with peak winds of 105 mph, and tracked southeast through Clark County, Missouri. It then continued across the Mississippi River into Hancock County, Illinois, impacting northern parts of Warsaw. This tornado persisted for about 1.3 miles, doing damage largely to numerous trees, with concentrated snapping including along the banks of the Mississippi River, as shown by drone footage. There also was damage to two gas station canopies along US Highway 61 in Missouri.

A storm survey team from the National Weather Service office in State College confirmed widespread microburst damage occurring across a 2 mile wide area in Dauphin and Middle Paxton Township, Pennsylvania. At approximately 7:21 PM EDT on Sunday, Jun 14, 2026 a severe thunderstorm began producing damaging straight line winds just north of Route 22 along the Susquehanna River, with multiple trees uprooted and snapped on properties along Kathryn Ave. Two trees damaged a fence and a shed as they fell. The storm and accompanying microburst travelled northeast over the next 5 minutes, snapping or uprooting at least 100 trees. Three very large trees fell across two cars and a home on Hecks Dr. The microburst produced tree damage as far north as Mountain Road, as far west as Garber Lane, and as far east as Fulton Rd. Several witnesses describe the storm as producing penny to quarter size hail followed by an opaque wall of heavy rain and wind. We thank the many homeowners who took the time to speak with us.

A brief EF1 tornado, with peak winds of 90 mph, developed just south of Pekin, IA, impacting areas from Pekin Community Schools east-southeast towards Linby, IA. At Pekin Schools, softwood trees were snapped above the base in a narrow area just north of the football field. There were also portions of a metal roof peeled off of an outbuilding. The tornado blew down a chain link fence near the softball diamond, then damaged one of the softball dugouts and depositing the debris along the trees southeast of the softball diamond. The tornado then moved east-southeast towards Linby, where several broken tree branches and sheared trees were reported, along with a hardwood tree being uprooted.

A thunderstorm that had been showing supercell characteristics 
across portions of west central Indiana moved east over Owen 
County. Rotation was observed but no reports had occurred across 
much of western Owen County. Then shortly after 9:40 pm the 
rotation began to strengthen as it approached US 231. Tornado 
touched down just east of US 231 where sporadic tree damage was 
noted with some larger limbs knocked down and a few upper trunks 
of trees snapped. The tornado crossed the White River and 
continued to strengthen. Numerous trees were uprooted and/or large
trunks of trees snapped along Macville Road in Owen County. Some 
of the trees fell on a house on Macville Road. All of this damage 
was consistent with an EF1 tornado. 

The tornado continued east into Monroe county with numerous tree 
damage along County Line Road. Further east along N Texas Ridge 
Road the roof of a single story was removed and blown out into a 
field along with two garages that were completely destroyed. The
amount of tree damage increased further to the east with damage 
along Moon Road and Brighton Road. Two houses along Brighton Road 
had portions of the roof panels removed. A metal garage in the 
same area had a quarter of the roof pulled back. All of this 
damage remained consistent with an EF1 tornado. The tornado 
strengthened further as it approached Bowman Road, where a house 
with a large attached barn/garage was damaged. The garage was 
completely destroyed and large portions of the roof were removed 
on the house. This damage was estimated to be primarily EF2 
strength. 

Additional damage to houses and outbuildings was found along 
Mount Pleasant Road with an increasing amount of tree damage. Some
of the most widespread and strongest tree damage was found 
further to the east along Buskirk Road. Large swaths of trees were
either snapped or uprooted. In addition, some debarking of trees 
was noted as well. A mobile home along Buskirk Road was completely
destroyed with all debris being blown to the east. This damage is
consistent with a higher end EF2 tornado. The tornado continued 
eastwards over Interstate 69 where continued widespread tree 
damage was observed. Further analysis using drone footage indicated additional debarking of hardwood trees near and east of I-69, consistent with EF3 damage.  Initially, we had to end the survey at the entrance of 
the Morgan Monroe State Forest at the interaction of Old State 
Road 37 and Forest Road where the amount of tree damage prevented 
the survey team from going any further.  However, satellite analysis later on was able to find tree damage all the wat to the Monroe County border.

On the evening of June 16, Emergency Management and Firefighters reported a brief tornado touchdown from a supercell that had a documented history of a rotating wall cloud. A member of the fire department reported seeing vegetation lifted in this area, indicative of a brief tornado touchdown. Because the tornado occurred over an open field with no damage indicators, this tornado will be ranked as an EF-U; unknown. Airspace restrictions prohibit further evaluation via drone.

The same storm that produced the EF-2 tornado in Bristol, IN continued eastward into LaGrange County. While radar suggested the correlation coefficient signature persisted between Bristol and this tornado (albeit weaker), damage was very sparse, and there was not enough confidence or evidence to definitively connect the two areas of concern. Due to a 10-mile separation, it was determined to treat these as two separate tornadoes.

The tornado in LaGrange paralleled SR 120, producing an impressive swath of tree damage and causing visible damage to barns and center pivots. Given the time elapsed between the storm and the ground survey, it is likely some homes had already been repaired. The circulation reached a maximum width of 0.75 miles on the north side of Shipshewana, with a maximum intensity estimated to be EF-1 at 100 mph. The tornado occluded on the western side of Twin Lakes before a broader swath of straight-line wind damage took over in the Howe, IN and Sturgis, MI areas.

This long-track tornado developed about 5 miles east of Waukon, IA and continued tracking ESE, crossing the Mississippi River at Lock and Dam 9. It continued southeast through Crawford County before lifting just before reaching the Wisconsin River. Nearly continuous tree damage occurred along its path, significant in some areas. Other damage included destruction of some farm outbuildings and minor damage to a few residences. Damage along the 33 mile path was mostly EF0 to EF1 in magnitude, with localized pockets of EF2 damage to trees and powerlines.

This tornado developed just to the southeast of Boscobel and exhibited a weak and diffuse path for much of its existence, with an RFD interacting with and disrupting the tornado circulation from eastern Grant County into Iowa County. The majority of the damage caused by this tornado in Grant County was EF0 with pockets of EF1 damage, consisting of significant tree damage and some heavily damaged farm outbuildings. The tornado intensified slightly into Iowa County as the RFD became more of a driver in the damage field.

This tornado touched down near S 600 W Road just north of the intersection of W 550 S Road before tracking northeast across mainly open farmland in western Newton County. The tornado damaged a farm outbuilding along with several trees near S 550 W Road consistent with 85 mph winds and an EF-0 rating. From there, the tornado continued northeast through the town of Morocco, where a corridor of tree damage occurred, including near the town park. Additional tree damage across the broader Morocco area was consistent with straight-line winds in excess of 60 mph. After exiting Morocco, the tornado crossed US-41 before turning to the north-northeast across open farmland, where damage was confined to mainly trees and irrigation pivots. The tornado ended just east of the intersection of E 300 N Road and N 300 E Road. No injuries or fatalities were reported with this tornado.
A brief tornado produced tree damage and sporadic roofing damage across the far northern portion of the Saddlebrook Farms subdivision near Grayslake.

Tornado appears to have started southwest of Ridgeway, hitting the Town of Ridgeway salt shed near Highway 18/151.  It then tracked to the southeast and destroyed a metal shed along County Road H.  Otherwise, sporadic tree damage was noted along the end of the path with rear flank downdraft winds occurring to the southwest-south of the of the path.  Some tree damage was noted east of the end of the path but appeared to fan out and not be a path near County Rd K and Mounds View Rd.

An EF-2 tornado occurred on the southwest side of Maysville during the early morning hours of June 18. The tornado began just west of Martha Comer Drive, snapping several hardwood tree trunks before moving across the southern portion of the Maysville Community College campus. The Kentucky Mesonet site on campus measured a wind gust of 114 mph. The tornado then tracked east and northeast across open field, eventually hitting several businesses along Kentucky Highway 9 (AA Highway), causing roof and structural damage. 

As the tornado approached East Maple Leaf Road, it quickly intensified. A couple of residences were severely damaged, including an outbuilding demolished with pieces and contents of the structure thrown between 100-200 feet. This includes a 690 pound four wheeler and a large cinder block. A dual axle trailer jacked up on a block with two zero turn mowers and various other outdoor equipment inside was pushed nearly 100 feet before being stopped by a cement barrier. A house suffered extensive roof damage. A property on the east side of East Maple Leaf Road was also heavily damaged with the debris in a convergent path here as well. This includes the roof and siding of a house, several snapped and uprooted hardwood trees, and a couple of hardwood fences posted well into the ground being pulled toward the circulation. Splatter was observed on the east and south sides of the home, further suggesting a cyclonic rotation. The tornado then took a left turn toward the northeast as it snapped more trees and destroyed another portion of a fence. Additionally, on the southern side of the tornado, a couple of large barns were heavily damaged with both roofs a total loss as outflow winds occurred on the south side of the tornado. As the tornado continued on a northeast track across a field, a metal outbuilding was pulled down a hill as the circulation neared. Additional tree damage was observed east of Hill City Road before the tornado dissipated. Sporadic tree damage was reported farther northeast toward the Ohio River as a result of outflow winds.

The National Weather Service in Wilmington would like to thank Mason County Emergency Management and the state of Kentucky Emergency Management for their assistance in completing this survey.

Originating in Beecher City within Effingham County, the tornado first touched down along E State Highway 33. The storm's initial path spanned approximately one-quarter mile in width, resulting in EF0 and EF1 level damage. This impact was characterized by the snapping and uprooting of large trees, alongside sporadic damage to grain silos and farm out-buildings, with notable effects observed near N 300th St on the outskirts of Beecher City.

Moving eastward through Shumway, the tornado crossed State Highway 32 and proceeded parallel to E 1800th Ave. Although the path width constricted to just over one-tenth of a mile, the storm intensified, producing EF-2 level damage. The increased strength resulted in hardwood and softwood tree trunks being snapped approximately two-thirds of the way up. Additionally, the tornado caused significant structural destruction, including the removal of a roof from a single-family home and the collapse of several farm outbuildings.

Upon reaching the northern outskirts of rural Effingham, the tornado intensified to EF-3 status as it traveled along E 1800th Ave. During this stage, the storm produced peak wind speeds estimated at 145 mph, leading to severe tree damage and the total destruction of one single-family home, which suffered complete exterior wall collapses.

Continuing its path along Effingham's northern perimeter, the EF-3 tornado maintained a width of one-tenth to one-quarter mile. Substantial structural damage occurred at a farmstead on E 1680th Ave, where several large outbuildings were demolished and a single-family home suffered a total roof uplift alongside partial exterior wall failure. Upon entering Effingham city limits and crossing US HWY 45, the storm destroyed a substantial metal building system after an X-brace failed on its eastern side. Nearby properties sustained further structural and severe tree damage, and the force of the winds threw a delivery van approximately 150 yards to the east.

After departing Effingham, the tornado tracked southeastward and broadened to a width of approximately one-third of a mile. As the storm crossed Interstate 70, it inflicted major damage to trees and caused total roof uplift at multiple single-family homes. The tornado then proceeded across the northern and eastern parts of Teutopolis, where it caused extensive structural destruction to a farmstead located near the HWY 40 and N 1950th St intersection. Impacts at this location included the complete destruction of several large barns and outbuildings, as well as the total uplift of a single-residence roof.  The tornadic storm maintained its EF-3 intensity as it moved eastward into rural Teutopolis, though its path narrowed to roughly one-tenth of a mile. Near the intersection of N 2100th St and E 1500th Ave, the storm produced peak wind speeds of 140 mph, resulting in the destruction of two single-family homes and significant damage to trees and outbuildings. Multiple non-life-threatening injuries were reported in this area.

As the tornado moved across the Effingham-Jasper county line, it continued on a southeastward trajectory while weakening to EF-2 intensity. With estimated wind speeds of approximately 120 mph, the storm caused moderate damage to outbuildings and trees, along with minor structural impacts to single-family residences.

The tornado continued to the southeast where it caused major roof damage to a two-story house, rolled an SUV, damaged an outbuilding, and snapped several large hardwood trees. Moving southeast toward E 1700th Ave, the storm snapped the top of another large hardwood and stripped shingles from a single-story residence, with further tree damage reported just north of that location. East of N 700th St, more tree damage occurred alongside shingle damage to a mobile home. As the tornado tracked further along E 1700th Ave, it damaged another outbuilding, two grain bins and additional trees before finally lifting approximately 0.25 miles east of N 800th St.

A special thanks is extended to Effingham County EMA for their assistance in supplying geo-referenced data for severely damaged buildings. We also wish to recognize the local agricultural community along E 1800th Ave in rural Effingham; their willingness to provide transportation was essential for navigating a section of the path obstructed by active utility restoration efforts.

An EF-1 Tornado wound through the valley along Route 4, where it uprooted and snapped numerous trees. It also warped solar panels, a metal shed, and took off some roofing before traveling up the hill where it lifted. A snapped tree collapsed a wooden structure.
A briefly strong EF-1 tornado touched down in the woods approaching York Hill Rd. The tornado crossed into the nearby ravine where damage trailed off.

A brief EF0 tornado touched down in Eden Isle, LA and moved east. Widespread branches and tree debris was found in Eden Isle along with a few houses with minor damage. One house had a failure at the garage where the wind looks to have been pushed into the garage. The tornado damaged businesses right near I-10 as it crossed over with a few more homes damaged and trees down in Lakeshore Village. 

The widespread light damage across Eden Isle did make this a difficult track, especially track width, to find. The additional damage was likely inflow from straight line winds and/or debris that was swirling out of the tornado.

The tornado first touched down in southern Menard county and moved southeast into Salisbury. In town it mainly did tree damage, but also damaged a garage and roof of an adjacent home. As it continued southeast into northern Springfield, it continued to do mainly tree damage. As it exited the city on the northeast side, it blew in the garage door of a business. As it moved east-southeast it continued to do only tree damage and actually followed the same path as the June 10th EF1 tornado. The tornado ended about 2 miles west of Mechanicsburg.

The National Weather Service completed a storm survey and determined that a tornado occurred during the early morning hours on June 18, 2026 in Scott County and Jefferson County Indiana and then crossed the river into Trimble County Kentucky.  The tornado was 1000 yards wide and 23.62 miles in length.  Maximum winds were EF2 130 mph.

The tornado first touched down on the northeast side of Austin, Indiana near the community park.  Several trees were damaged with twisted tops or brought down entirely in the park.  Some fencing and bleacher damage was also observed at the ball fields.  The tornado continued across rural portions of Scott county just north of state road 256 with tree damage along the way.  The most notable damage started occurring in extreme eastern Scott county north of Wooster along Blanton Road.  Drone footage had shown a clear path in the woods of extensive tree damage with several house structures also having damage south of Hardy Lake.  High end EF1 winds around 110 mph began here.

The tornado continued into western Jefferson County Indiana along Henry road where the tornado gained size and strength.  Several farms north of Henry road had barns totally destroyed with extensive tree damage.  Some residences also were completely demolished.  Max sustained winds of EF2 120 mph occurred north of the Republican, Kent, and Hanover communities to the west of Madison.  The tornado dropped over the cliff past state road 56 toward Clifty Creek Generating Station, where the tornado gained strength.  The maximum winds for the entire tornado occurred at the power plant at EF2 130 mph.  At this location, a steel electrical transmission line was completely toppled and mangled.  The power lines dropped into the Ohio River and closed river traffic at Madison Indiana due to this tornado.  In Jefferson County, at least one injury was reported and at least 6 cattle were killed from the tornado.

The tornado then crossed the Ohio River into Trimble County, Kentucky near Milton.  Several trees and campers along Coopers Bottom Road received extensive damage with maximum winds at EF1 110 mph.  The tornado ended just along US Highway 421 near Milton with no additional damage observed to the east of the Highway.

The National Weather Service would like to extend a big thank you to Scott County Emergency Management, Jennings Township Fire Department, Jefferson County Emergency Management, Trimble County Emergency Management, the Indiana Department of Homeland Security, and the many helpers that assisted Emergency Management with damage assessments and mapping provided to the NWS to assist with this survey.  Thanks also goes to the many helpful homeowners who gave their tornado accounts and gave access to their damaged properties to allow for a complete documented tornado survey.

The first damage produced by the tornado occurred on Texas Gas Road, where a large tree was uprooted and other smaller trees were downed. Farther east along Cole Lane, an attached garage was destroyed and a large tree was downed onto a house. In addition, a roof was lifted from another garage and several trees were snapped at their trunks.

The tornado strengthened and proceeded east near East Laughery Creek Road, where it completely destroyed a house and two outbuildings. Debris from these buildings was strewn east along the path of the tornado across a large field. Based on this damage, estimated wind speeds were around 130 MPH in this area, and the damage also resulted in a Tornadic Debris Signature on the Wilmington, Ohio radar at this time. The tornado continued toward Alta Vista Ave, where a large number of hardwood trees were snapped.

The tornado then moved across Laughery Creek, producing significant tree damage along and near Laughery Creek and in wooded areas along Hartford Pike where numerous trees were snapped. Along Holmes Hill Road, more tree damage was observed along with the roof being lifted off an outbuilding. 

On Thuermer Hollow Road, more trees were damaged and a roof was lifted off a barn. Along State Road 56, additional roof damage from a barn and damage to large healthy trees was noted. Farther east on the Indiana side of the Ohio River, numerous trees were knocked down at a campground. The tornado weakened as it moved across the Ohio River into Boone County, Kentucky. The last observed damage from this tornado was noted on Belleview Road, where large tree branches were snapped.

The National Weather Service would like to thank the Dearborn County, Indiana Emergency Management Agency,  the Ohio County, Indiana Emergency Agency and Boone County, Kentucky Emergency Management Agency for their assistance and support with this damage survey.

The National Weather Service conducted a damage survey and confirmed a tornado in Carroll County, Kentucky and Switzerland County, Indiana during the early morning hours on June 18th, 2026. The tornado was determined to be an EF1 with maximum winds of 100 MPH.

The first sign of tornadic damage was just east of Patton Hollow Rd in Switzerland County, IN, where numerous trees were damaged. The tornado would continue SE, where notable damage occurred at two properties located off of E SR-56. Several large, hardwood trees were uprooted and/or snapped at the base. Additionally, both of these homes observed a substantial loss of roofing materials, as well as damage to their wooden porches. 

The tornado would cross the Ohio River, with the next area of damage appearing along US Route 42 along the Ohio River where several wooden electrical power lines were downed and extensive tree damage occurred. Just to the west of Tom Harris Road, a hillside had extensive tree damage as well. The tornado continued across rural areas east of Carrollton where additional damage occurred along State Route 36. Here several power lines were downed, along with extensive tree damage. The tornado continued near the Easterday community near Boone Road and State Route 36. Several tree lines and residences had damage. The tornado then continued along Dividing Ridge Road, crossed Interstate 71, and then slowly became weaker along Ghent Eagle, Briar Fork, and Indian Creek Roads. Beyond Indian Creek Road, no additional damage was observed in Carroll County.

The National Weather Service would like to thank Switzerland County Emergency Management, Carroll County Emergency Management and NWS Louisville forecast office for the escort and assistance into the affected communities to help complete the damage survey.

The tornado touched down about 4 miles southwest of Bethany in northeast Christian County where it snapped a softwood tree trunk and removed large branches from hardwood trees. It continued east, crossing the county line into Moultrie County and damaging more trees along its path. It lifted near County Road 300 N, about 2 miles south of Bethany.

This brief tornado caused damage at Kuipers Family Farm where a large portion of the south-facing roof of a barn was peeled up with debris blown northeast. Several small trees were also snapped on the property. Additional damage occurred at the Acquaviva Winery where a portion of the roof of a large pole barn was peeled off.

The first evidence of the tornado was found on Landings Way where several trees were snapped at their trunks. Farther east, along Oakbrook Road near Pleasant Valley Road, additional tree damage was found along with minor damage to building fascia. The tornado proceeded east through residential areas of Oakbrook near Sentry Drive and Thunder Ridge Drive where a few larger hardwood trees were snapped and minor roof damage was noted.

The tornado progressed east, uprooting trees and snapping tree trunks along Hopeful Road, Surfwood Drive, and Rosetta Drive. The tornado then crossed Interstates 71/75 where it lifted a portion of the roof of one commercial building and caused additional roof damage to a second building. A large power pole was snapped near the intersection of US-42 and Dream Street and a local business had its sign destroyed. This is where the tornado is estimated to have reached peak intensity, with winds around 100 MPH. 

The tornado then continued east into additional residential areas from here. Large tree limbs were downed along Hollywood Drive and there were numerous trees and large branches down along Ann Street, Lee Street, and Julia Avenue. The home near Ann Street had a large tree fall onto it, causing minor roof damage. 

The tornado continued southeast, crossing into Kenton County, snapping several trees at residences along Autumn Road. The final known instance of tornadic damage was on Tallwood Circle, where multiple large branches were downed. 

The National Weather Service would like to thank the Boone County, Kentucky Emergency Management Agency and the Kenton County, Kentucky Emergency Management Agency for their assistance and support with this damage survey.

The first evidence of tornadic damage occurred on a property just east of Clarks Creek where several trees were uprooted or snapped. The tornado would continue east towards Baton Rouge Rd, where several more hardwood trees had large branches broken off, with tree debris thrown onto both sides of the road. Additionally, a barn was completely destroyed in the same area. Sporadic tree damage would continue along Baton Rouge Rd, eventually leading to another barn where the walls completely collapsed and the roof blown off. The damage to these outbuildings was consistent with EF1 damage, with maximum winds around 90 mph. Just a bit farther down the road, another outbuilding had its sheet metal roof completely ripped off, with pieces of sheet metal thrown ~50 yards into the nearby field. Some of the siding was also peeled off. 

The damage path would continue along portions of Baton Rouge Rd, with extensive tree damage noted leading up to the intersection of I-75. Most of the tree damage was primarily large branches that were broken off, but there was one hardwood tree that was uprooted. Just east of I-75, additional tree damage occurred, including some wooden power poles that were snapped. 

The area of most concentrated damage would occur in several neighborhoods just east of US-25. On Ridgelea Dr, there were multiple large, healthy trees that were uprooted and/or snapped at the base. On Humes Ridge Rd, more large trees and wooden power poles were snapped. The most significant damage occurred near the end of the tornadic path on Waterworks Rd, where a standalone, multi-car garage had the majority of its roof ripped off. Multiple sections of the garage observed a significant loss of its cinderblock exterior walls, including some minor damage to the interior walls between car ports. Debris from the garage was spread out into the nearby field. Given the structural integrity of the garage, it’s expected that wind speeds up to 95 mph were observed in this part of the tornado track, which is consistent with EF1 damage. Finally, some minor tree damage was observed in the field just off to the east before the tornado lifted. 

The National Weather Service office would like to thank Grant County Emergency Management Agency, State of Kentucky Emergency Management, and the Williamstown Fire Department for their assistance with this damage survey.

An EF0 tornado with winds of 85 MPH tracked north to south across Arabi, LA in St. Bernard Parish. This was confirmed via eyewitness videos, along with debris thrown to the SE and convergent debris in that direction. Almost all of the damage was shingles off well built homes, fence damage and large branches down. Three houses had a good part of their roof removed. Two were older houses, one built in the 50s. One house had a car port attached to the roof which is where the failure occurred. The third was abandoned and neighbors confirmed it also had extensive termite damage. That and rot was observed on the roof. Given that well built homes had minor damage and the damage on the three houses were from older roofs, the rating is an 85 MPH EF0.

This tornado track has been updated based on high-resolution satellite imagery and storm chaser video. 

This tornado started in the vicinity of N 8th Road near Sandy Creek. Distinct swirl marks are evident as the tornado tracked northeast before tracking almost due east and crossing E 9th Road roughly one third of a mile south of IL-17. The tornado then continued on a northeasterly path, impacting a residence on IL-17 where it caused some roof damage, snapped a large hardwood tree about one-third of the way from the top, and downed a wooden electrical pole. The tornado then continued along IL-17, destroying multiple machine sheds in the 900 block, with debris strewn northeastward toward E 10th Rd. Storm chaser video shows at least three fast-moving subvortices as the tornado continued northeast and crossed E 10th Rd. Here, high-resolution Sentinel satellite imagery reveals significant cycloidal markings, widening to approximately 500 yards as the tornado tracked across multiple fields before appearing to weaken rapidly and lift near N 10th Rd just west of the Livingston County line.

A well-defined damage path of an EF-0 tornado was identified on high-resolution satellite imagery over rural, inaccessible parts of southeast St. Charles Parish. The tornado touched down near Bayou des Allemands and tracked north-northwest over rural, inaccessible marshland. While the majority of damage along this path was marsh vegetation, a narrow swath of trees were evidently damaged/displaced which is the basis for its EF-0 rating. The tornado continued north-northwest with the narrow damage path becoming less defined with time. The tornado dissipated east of Bayou Gauche after being on the ground for over 3 miles.

This brief, weak, and narrow tornado began as a highly visible funnel cloud just west of Osseo. It touched down at Merchants Baseball Field off US Highway 10 where it destroyed a storage garage and caused tree damage. The tornado likely lifted temporarily as it tracked southeast and crossed the highway, with the next downstream damage occurring off W 5th St near Spruce Rd. In this area, it damaged a couple sheds, trees, and a power pole before dissipating.

An EF-1 tornado touched down over inaccessible areas west of Bayou Dularge and tracked northeast toward Crozier Drive. Predominantly minor to moderate patches of tree damage were visible on high resolution satellite imagery along its path which were collocated with a tornado debris signature on Climavision radar V014. Trees were more evidently displaced and damaged as the tornado exited the inaccessible marsh and forested areas and moved over Crozier Drive. A NWS survey team observed two homes on Crozier Drive that had significant roof loss and at least one exterior wall collapsed for both homes. The tornado continued northeast across Bayou Dularge Rd and into more inaccessible marsh and forest vegetation where more minor damage was evident on satellite imagery. The end point of this tornado is estimated and it's possible it extended further northeast though no conclusive evidence of damage was identified.

The brunt of the damage was to a double wide manufactured home that was bolted to a poured basement foundation. Unfortunately there was a fatality at this residence. Most of the debris from the home and outbuildings was scattered to the northeast. The debris could be found six miles to the northeast, but there wasn't additional structural damage in this path.

At approximately 6:08 AM, a tornado developed east of Stanton,
Iowa, near 230th Street and Q Avenue, and moved northeast. The
tornado produced tree damage on the west side of Viking Lake,
including large broken limbs and uprooted trees, with estimated
winds of 70 to 85 mph. The tornado then crossed to the east side
of Viking Lake, where it uprooted two trees, brought down
numerous large limbs, caused minor siding and roof damage to a
home near 230th Street and Raspberry Drive, and snapped
approximately 10 pine tree trunks near S Avenue and Aldersgate
Drive. Based on this damage, winds were estimated at 90 mph. The
tornado then continued northeast, collapsing the walls of an
outbuilding, snapping a tree trunk, and bringing down power lines
near U.S. Highway 24 and T Avenue. Based on this damage, peak
winds were estimated around 105 mph. The tornado then lofted
grain bins from over a mile away into the interchange of Highway
71 and Highway 34. The tornado dissipated at approximately
6:16 AM.

A fast-moving QLCS brought sporadic tree and farm structure damage to portions of northern Warren county. Damage began near West County Road 850N with an uprooted tree with additional minor damage to a barn after the tornado crossed US 41. The most significant damage was noted near the intersection of Rainsville Road and State Road 26 where multiple trees were downed and corn fields showed clear convergence. The tornado tracked mostly through open fields with additional tree damage noted on North 200E and North 300E before dissipating just south of the Benton county line.

NWS ground survey along with public reports determined that an EF0 tornado with a 200 yard wide path initially touched down in a wooded area at the end of County Road H-522 to the southeast of Eminence.  The tornado damaged a barn then both broke and uprooted trees as it crossed Highway H and  along Highway NN to the Rocky Falls Shut In area off County Road NN-526.

The tornado touched down near Christianburg Road with extensive tree damage within a large grove of trees. The tornado then moved into Hilltop Camp where it caused additional extensive tree damage along a path with the center line of the tornado tracking just to the southwest of a group of buildings. A steel frame door was sheared off a building and pushed to the northwest with roof damage on the buildings also strewn about in numerous directions. The tornado continued through another tree grove before crossing Hamilton Creek Road and finally impacting a home near the 6700 block of Hamilton Creek Road before dissipating.

An EF-3 tornado touched down 2.5 miles south of Dix along Hwy 37. It quickly intensified and lead to complete destruction of several mobile homes leading to 2 fatalities along July Road and Ranch Lane. A few power poles were snapped and a couple sheds were damaged or destroyed. The degree of tree damage along the path was impressive including dozens that were snapped or uprooted. The tornado crossed over into Wayne County Illinois and was on the ground just over 1 mile before lifting 6 miles northwest of Wayne City. Thank you to the Jefferson County EMA for their assistance with the survey.
NWS storm survey found very clear tornadic damage (EF-1) east of Kinmundy, with supporting video showing a multi-vortex tornado in that location.

The tornado touched down west of County Road 300 E before damaging a barn just to the east with part of the roof ripped off. The tornado caused extensive damage to a grove of trees between County Road 300E and 375E with additional damage to 3 structures along 375E.
