A National Weather Service Storm Survey team has determined that an EF-0 tornado with maximum estimated winds of 85 mph occurred in Trumbull and Mahoning Counties on July 21, 2026. The tornado extended for over 6 miles with a maximum path width of about 100 yards. 

The tornado formed in the southeast portion of Liberty Township in Trumbull County, Ohio at the northwest corner of Hubbard Road (US Route 62) and Logan Gate Road, where a couple tree branches were snapped. The tornado continued southeast along Applegate Road, crossing into Hubbard, causing more tree damage and some minor roof damage to a residence, exhibiting 85 mph winds. Dozens of trees were damaged further southeast in a heavily wooded area, as the tornado crossed into Mahoning County and into the Youngstown city limits. The tornado entered the McGuffey Heights neighborhood with tree damage observed in the vicinity of Jacobs Road and Orrin Avenue and extending southeast onto Gerwig Avenue. The tornado reached the vicinity of Coitsville-Hubbard Road (Ohio State Route 616) and McGuffey Road causing more minor tree damage and flipping a wagon that was attached to a heavier trailer. The tornado reached the vicinity of North Hubbard Road and Johnson Road, prompting more minor tree damage. The tornado intensified once again to 85 mph along Wilson Lane with a concentrated area of large snapped tree branches that caused minor damage to a residence. The tornado then uprooted several trees along Oak Street before continuing southeast to the Ohio/Pennsylvania state line, north of US Route 422.

From here, this tornado continued southeast into Lawrence County, Pennsylvania. Please see the Public Information Statement from the National Weather Service office in Pittsburgh for details for that portion of the tornado.

In summary, for Ohio, this EF-0 tornado had estimated maximum wind gusts of 85 mph in southwest Hubbard and southeastern Coitsville Township and was on the ground for about 16 minutes, extending for over 6 miles with a maximum path width of about 100 yards.

The National Weather Service would like to thank Trumbull County and Mahoning County Emergency Management Agencies with their assistance in the storm survey.

THE NATIONAL WEATHER SERVICE IN COORDINATION WITH LOCAL AND STATE
PUBLIC SAFETY OFFICIALS CONFIRMED A SHORT LIVED AND INTERMITTENT
EF0 TORNADO THAT DEVELOPED IN PURCHASE, WESTCHESTER COUNTY, NY AND
TRAVELED EAST NORTHEAST TOWARD RYE BROOK, NY. THIS CONFIRMATION
WAS STRENGTHENED BY RADAR EVIDENCE OF A ROTATING THUNDERSTORM WITH
NON- METEORLOGICAL DEBRIS (LIKELY LEAVES AND SMALL BRANCHES)
LOFTED SEVERAL THOUSAND FEET ABOVE THE GROUND.

THE TORNADO LIKELY BEGAN ON MANHATTANVILLE COLLEGE CAMPUS WHERE
IT UPROOTED SEVERAL TREES IN ADDITION TO SNAPPING LARGE BRANCHES.
THE TORNADO LIKELY LIFTED BEFORE TOUCHING DOWN TO THE SOUTHEAST
AND SHEARING OFF THE TOPS OF TREES AND UPROOTING A FEW TREES ON
LINCOLN AVENUE NEAR LODEN LANE. THE TORNADO LIKELY LIFTED ONCE
AGAIN, BEFORE MAKING FINAL TOUCHDOWN TO THE EAST NORTHEAST NEAR
LAWRIDGE DRIVE AND DOWNING A FEW TREES AND WIRES. THE TORNADO
LIKELY LIFTED ONE LAST TIME AND DISSIPATED BEFORE THE STORM MADE
ITS WAY OVER THE NY/CT STATE LINE, WITH A SPOTTER REPORTING TREE
BRANCH AND LEAF DEBRIS LITTERING DOWN ON THE HUTCHINSON PARKWAY
SHORTLY BEFORE 420PM.

THE NATIONAL WEATHER SERVICE WOULD LIKE TO THANK WESTCHESTER
COUNTY EMERGENCY MANAGEMENT, HARRISON NY POLICE DEPARTMENT,
CONNECTICUT DIVISION OF EMERGENCY MANAGAEMENT AND HOMELAND
SECURITY, BROADCAST MEDIA, AND SPOTTERS WHO SHARED VIDEO AND
PHOTOGRAPHIC EVIDENCE, AND THE GENERAL PUBLIC WHO SHARED REPORTS
THROUGH SOCIAL MEDIA, IN ASSISTING THE SURVEY AND FORMULATING THIS
PRELIMINARY DAMAGE REPORT.

A brief tornado occurred along Railroad Trestle Road that caused tree damage, including snapping large tree trunks and branches. Fortunately, no structures were damaged from this tornado. The tornado lifted after 1 minute on the ground, with very little damage seen at the triangular intersection of Louisville Nashville Turnpike and Railroad Trestle Road.

The National Weather Service confirmed a brief EF-1 tornado touchdown in northeast Casey County and northwest Lincoln County, Kentucky. A briefly tornadic storm first produced a tornado in far northeastern Casey County along Kentucky Highway 78 just north of the intersection with Kentucky Highway 906 around 5:37 PM EDT. Several large tree trunks were snapped near the intersection of a home on a hillside next to an open field. Estimated wind speeds from the tree damage were observed at 95 mph which is EF-1 damage.

The tornado continued moving NE parallel to Kentucky Highway 78 and damaged a barn just downstream of the hillside home that was also in the middle of an open field. The north-facing roof slope had large sections of roofing ripped off, with estimated tornado wind speeds around 95 mph as well. Then, the tornado continued moving NE snapping large trunks and tree limbs on the southern facing side of a small forest next to the open field. The tornado here slightly increased in strength, with estimated winds here near 100 mph, or high-end EF-1 damage.

Beyond the barn, the tornado continued its track NE through the open field with scattered tree cover. It began weakening as it moved towards Black Pike in far western Lincoln County west of Hustonville. At 5:39 PM EDT, power poles were snapped along with additional large tree limbs snapped with estimated winds of 85 mph, or a high end EF-0. Shortly after, the tornado lifted and no other tornadic damage was observed.

The National Weather Service would like to thank the Casey Emergency Management teams for assistance with this damage survey.

Early Monday April 27, 2026, a supercell thunderstorm moving across southern Leavenworth County Kansas resulted in a brief, EF 1 tornado at 3:31 AM CDT. The tornado began just west of US 24, south of Tonganoxie, between Honey Creek Road and north of Hemphill Road. EF 1 damage to an outbuilding and trees were surveyed just west of US 24. The tornado continued across open country east of US 24 before causing EF-0 damage to an outbuilding and power poles near the intersection of Hemphill Road and 214th St. Special thanks to Leavenworth County Emergency Management for the survey assistance.

A tornado occurred just east of Feesburg during the mid afternoon of July 21. Damage was first observed along State Route 505 where multiple pieces of a roof were blown off of an outbuilding along with a tree being downed across the road. The tornado then continued moving to the southeast along Day Road where numerous trees were snapped and downed along a convergent path. Additional tree damage occurred along Eden Road up to Daugherty Marks Road before the tornado dissipated.

The National Weather Service would like to thank the Brown County Emergency Management Agency for their assistance with this storm damage survey.

The first evidence of tornadic damage was observed at the Pierce Reserve & Trails on Pond Run Road, where numerous large tree limbs were knocked down. The tornado strengthened as it moved southeast onto Mott Road, where roof damage was observed at a two story home along with numerous trees being snapped in an adjacent wooded area. Winds in this area were likely near 90 mph, which corresponds to EF-1 on the Enhanced Fujita Scale. Tree damage was common and in a very convergent path along Fagins Run Road and Wilson Dunham Hill Road. While damage became more sporadic farther southeast, additional tree damage within the convergent tornadic path was reported at a residence on OH-132 and Wildfire Way. Large tree limbs were also knocked down along New Richmond Nicholsville Road, and this is where this tornado appears to have ended. 

The National Weather Service would like to thank the Clermont County Ohio Emergency Management Agency and Pierce Township Fire Department for their assistance with this storm damage survey.

A brief small spin up tornado occurred on the western edge of Wayne County in the South Canaan vicinity.

A heavy shower starting exhibiting loose rotation while crossing the Archbald Mountain ridge. As the shower dropped in elevation, rotation quickly tightened to spin up a short-lived tornado. It took out well-established apple trees in an orchard, while causing siding and soffit damage to a couple houses as well as destroying a hunter shed. The tornado lost some intensity while tracking over and then past Lake Quinn, before falling apart shortly after Easton Turnpike.

Storm chaser report of a tornado in the Zoar area from a tall, skinny thunderstorm. The tornado crossed highway 47 between Neopit and Zoar, producing some tree damage. Location and path determined from photos, video, and radar time-matching. Winds estimated to be around 70 mph.
Several reports of tornadoes in the Stratford area from tall, skinny thunderstorms. Location and path determined from photos, video, and radar time-matching.

Tree damage began near the northwest terminus of Gum Street and
continued east-southeast toward Morann Avenue (PA-153). Several
pine trees were snapped off halfway up between Gum Street and
Hemlock Street along with minor damage to a few structures. Upon
crossing Morann Avenue, the tornado moved across N Railroad street
and continued to produce extensive damage to trees and power
lines. A single wide mobile home and adjacent vehicle were shifted
slightly northeast as winds surged around the south side of the
circulation. Farther northeast toward the intersection of N
Railroad St and Hale Rd, a chimney was ripped off the side of a
house and a couple trees fell northwest/upwind. Seeing trees fall
opposite the direction of the tornado's motion provided the
confidence to lean toward the upper end of damage indicators,
making this a high-end EF-1 at 110mph. 

Remarkably, there was only very minor damage to many of the 
structures in the path of this tornado, but extensive snapping of 
trees. In particular, the forested area southeast of N Railroad
Street and southwest of Hale Rd suffered extensive tree fall.
Dozens to perhaps hundreds of trees were knocked over and/or
snapped off. The camp owner at the top of the hill at the
southeast edge of the forested area remarked that he could not
previously see the mountain to his northwest. His previously
"shaded" camp now had a much improved view, he said. Again, little
to no damage occurred to any of the structures (campers and a
cabin) at the camp, but extensive tree damage occurred. The 
tornado then briefly lifted/stopped producing damage to the 
southeast of a hilltop as it crossed an open field. Damage resumed
as the tornado moved back into a forested area along Hale Rd 
toward Sonia Ln. Extensive tree and powerline damage was observed 
along that stretch with a convergent pattern of tree fall. The 
damage became much more sporadic as the circulation crossed 
Moshannon Creek, marking the end of the tornado path.

NWS State College would like to send a sincere thanks to
Clearfield County Department of Emergency Services and the
Houtzdale Fire Company for their assistance with today's survey.
Additional surveys may be conducted in the coming days for this
severe weather event and additional Public Information Statements
will be sent as needed.

Damage from this tornado commenced off of Darlington road with large branches down and a few uprooted trees.  Given limited road access there were just spotty reports as the storm traveled east through Moxahala Ridge.  The most significant damage of the storm occurred on Old River road where an estimated 100-200 down hardwood trees were snapped, uprooted, or large limbs knocked over.  The peak tornado intensity was located here and just across the Muskingum river on the property of Shelly and Sands where part of an outbuilding roof was lifted.  The storm lifted as it skirted through Duncan Falls, OH causing large limbs to come down.  Tree damage was reported on both sides of the river south of Durant road of State Route 60 before entering Duncan Falls. 

The National Weather Service would like to thank Muskingum county Emergency Management Agency for all their assistance.  We would also like to thank a media station out of Columbus Ohio for providing drone footage. 

These are the 32nd and 33rd tornadoes on record for Muskingum county since 1880.  The last tornado to affect Muskingum county was June 6th 2024.  With these tornadoes, this brings our office count for the year up to 27 tornadoes.  The average number per year is eight.  For a state breakdown this is what we have:

Ohio: 5
West Virginia: 2
Pennsylvania: 21

A weak EF0 tornado commenced just north of Fultonham near Workman road.  Video evidence of a funnel cloud was captured just prior to this touchdown near the Muskingum - Licking county line.  The twister then had intermittent touchdowns as it moved east southeast through the southern part of the county.  Most of the damage was single trees down and large branches.  The amount of damaged trees that were visible during the survey was less than 50 for the duration of the track.  This number could increase pending additional reports over the coming days.  The storm traveled east downing a few trees in Avondale on the west side of state route 93.   When it arrived near Baughman run and Butterbean ridge area large limbs and a few hardwood trees were observed to be down.  The last observed damage point was along Buttermilk Road east of Gaysport where large limbs were down along Buttermilk road.  No structural damage nor injuries were observed or reported. 

The National Weather Service would like to thank Muskingum county Emergency Management Agency for all their assistance.

Multiple reports of thin tornado in open field northwest of Knox. This matches location of track apparent on Sentinel satellite. No currently known damage indicators along this track.
Intermittent tornado path that produced damage to roof of home along with convergent signature in the corn field.

Drone footage and on ground surveys indicate swath of damage to mostly large white pines of approximately 1 to 3 feet in diameter. Damage path is cyclonic in nature, with varying damage path directions along within the northern half of the polygon.
Video and radar evidence suggest a waterspout moved on shore at Shot Point. No surveyable damage was found by storm survey team.

A second confirmed EF1 tornado occurred within a Quasi-Linear Convective System (QLCS) at 145 PM EDT on Tuesday July 21. Though this line caused scattered damage in general, a tornadic convergent pattern was evident starting near the Shafer Wylie Horton Road intersection. It nearly paralleled Wylie Horton Road for a few miles, and then caused its heaviest damage to a farm just west of Bowbell Road. A haybarn lost its roof and most of its walls, with material strewn across the street and wrapped around a telephone pole. A roof section was lofted at least 100 yards. Roof material from other outbuildings, and the top of a silo, were removed. A section of cinder block wall collapsed from tornadic inflow. The tornado also uprooted a large section of trees just east of Bowbell Road, while departing to mainly south of Wylie Horton Road. The tornado weakened before crossing Highway 235, with the path becoming discontinuous. The tornado ended around 152 PM EDT.

A tornado descended on the 5100 block of Back Creek Road. Here
there was roof and siding damage to the house and outbuildings. On
this farm property and to the east through unpopulated forest,
thousands of trees were downed (80 to 90 percent at one point just
east of property), many of which were hardwoods 1-2 feet thick
snapped at the trunk.

Once the tornado crossed the ridge into Virginia, notable tree
damage occurred across the northernmost part of Wilde Acres, VA.
Damage was first visible on Otter Trail and extended southeast
with damage visible on each street until stopping near Fawn Drive.
While tree damage was visible throughout this path, the greatest
concentration of damage was on Cardinal Drive. Trees were observed
uprooted, snapped, or sheared off at the top. Considerable leaf
and small branch debris was observed throughout the entire path.

The National Weather Service thanks both Hampshire County WV
Office of Emergency Management and Frederick County VA Emergency
Management Division for their assistance with this survey.

A tornado briefly touched down near Seneca Rocks just after 7 PM.
Damage was limited almost entirely to trees. About 30 to 50
percent of trees were damaged on property in the 400 block of
Thunder Road, with trees mostly uprooted in a convergent pattern.
The tornado tracked east-northeast. None of the farm buildings
sustained significant damage, nor did the house on the property.
The tornado crossed the road and tracked up a hillside across the
street with continued tree damage before dissipating after about
two minutes.

Scattered to numerous large trees uprooted and snapped along the
path that started along Kiser Gap Road a half mile north of the
intersection with US Route 33. The tornado tracked east-
northeast. Where it crossed the 1600 block of Troublesome Valley
Road it snapped a tree down over the road on a vehicle. The driver
was extracted uninjured.

Substantial tree damage continued over the 1000 to 2300 blocks of
Corner Road, and 6500 to 7000 blocks of Sweedlin Valley Road and
the 300 block of Redbud Hill Lane. The tornado then tracked
through an unpopulated, wooded area across the ridge/state line. It
reached the 24300 block of Gochenour Lane 3 miles southwest of
Criders. The damage continued up Gobble Mountain before lifting.

In summary, thousands of trees were downed along this rural 10.5
mile path. In peak intensity areas, most of the trees in the path
were uprooted or snapped. Structural damage was mainly from tree
falls, although there was some wind damage to siding and
outbuildings noted.

The National Weather Service thanks the Pendleton County Office of
Emergency Management for their invaluable assistance to this
survey.

A tornado touched down on a farm in the 19300 block of
Mechanicsville Road. Numerous trees on this property had their
tops snapped off, with farm equipment (trailers and carts) tossed
about. In the woods surrounding the property, a path of trees were
snapped and uprooted in a convergent pattern. About 50 to 60
percent of the trees in the path were blown over. The tornado
tracked through unpopulated woods and fields for about a mile
before reaching another farm in the 19600 block of Cold Spring
Road. Here, additional trees were uprooted or snapped at the top.

The tornado continued east and crossed the 800 and 900 blocks of
Ridge Road where approximately 50 trees were downed, one on a
chicken coop structure. Further tree damage occurred along the
1900 and 2000 blocks of New Market Depot Road where several trees
were uprooted and snapped, with numerous large branches snapped
down. The final noted damage was to the 500 block of Hayneswood
Lane where one large tree was uprooted and several large branches
were snapped.

The NWS thanks local broadcast media for their assistance in
collecting damage reports.

A tornado briefly touched down just west of Coppinville Junior High School. The tornado damaged an awning on the westernmost building of the school and tossed some debris around the lawn. The tornado then crossed a wooded area spapping some branches before lifting northwest of Thornbird Loop. The track was flown by drone and video footage also captured the tornado. Damage was minor, consistent with EF0 strength with maximumwind estimated to be 70 mph.

The National Weather Service in Pittsburgh concluded an EF1
tornado formed just north of Moraine State Park on Sunday
June 14th.

The tornado started near Patterson Road, west of West Park
Road, then moved east-southeast, snapping large branches and a few trees near
the trunk along Cornelius Road. The largest amount of tree damage was
observed on West Park Road where an old barn roof was lifted off and
numerous large trees lost larger branches.

Toward the end of its track, the tornado curved northeastward near Mount Union and Reichert Roads before weakening.

NWS Pittsburgh has confirmed a brief tornado southeast of Derry, PA from a storm on July 18, 2026.

Sporadic damage primarily to trees was noted along a path beginning near Carey Ln and continuing southeast across Matson Rd through heavily wooded areas.  A review of aerial photography has helped identify impacted areas inaccessible by foot.

At its peak, damage appears consistent with wind of up to 70 mph.

Beyond this point, no damage was evident.  However, the path, magnitude and width of the tornado is subject to change pending additional reported damage coming to light.

Drone footage shared from Knox County Emergency Manager shows a swath of damage west of Windmill Road in Knox County associated with a Tornado. The footage shows some large limbs knocked down to the west of high-tension power lines. Then to the east some missing or pulled up metal roof panels of an outbuilding are observed in the video. The strongest damage was observed closer to Windmill Road where large limbs of several hardwood trees were destroyed. Then a metal outbuilding had the roof completely removed and lofted. Panels are observed to the north of the building and the debris field to the east of the structure supports tornadic activity. Based on satellite imagery believe the structure was open to the southeast allowing for an easier inflow of wind into the structure which allowed the roof to be lofted. This resulted in a lowering of the wind speed given the damage indicator. A brief TDS is also evident on radar directly over this location. The tornado then lifted as it approached Windmill Road with some large limbs down along the road. No additional damage was evident to the east of the road.

A storm persisted over Crawford County around 6:00pm. This storm intensified into a supercell over the county, before heading into northern Venango County around 6:34pm. With ample low-level rotation as evidenced by local radar, the cell proceeded to touch down at 6:37pm in Diamond, PA. The most evidence of tornadic activity was noted by a hardwood tree down in a tree-line north of town with some tree tops snapped by wind. This was the tied for the strongest damage indicator, with 80mph wind estimated. Some medium sized branches were snapped off trees in Diamond-proper, but most damage observed was from a prior storm which moved through on June 14th, 2026. The damage direction from this tornado was observed from northeast-to-southwest, while the June damage direction was east-to-west. Additional tree damage was observed on the east side of PA-428 before the tornado moved into a wooded area. A large tree was down in a similar direction on Goodwin Road, which signaled the final damage on the tornado track, with estimated wind speeds also at 80mph. This will go down as a 80mph EF-0, that lasted 2 minutes and traveled about one mile.

Venango County now has a total of 10 tornadoes dating back to 1950. The last tornado that occurred in Venango County Pennsylvania was on June 14, 2026. This was an EF-0 tornado that touched down east of Diamond.

The tornado began along Howells Ferry rd near Grider rd as a weak EF-0 bringing down a couple branches resulting in minor damage across two properties. The tornado then continued southeast across Carlisle Dr and strengthened as it approached Central Blvd and Mississippi St. south of Howells Ferry Rd. Several large uprooted hardwood trees were noted within this area with  more widespread small to large branches snapped throughout several roads within the community. The tornado then continued east towards Moffett Rd as it likely moved along Moffett before resulting in a few sporadic uprooted trees near a water treatment plant on the north side of Moffett Rd. The tornado likely weakened as it destroyed two businesses signs before dissipating near Northview Dr.
Several reports of tornadoes in the Tigerton area from a tall, skinny thunderstorm. Location and path determined from photos, video, and radar time-matching.

The tornado began in northern Christian County in the Griswold Conservation Area, causing extensive tree damage throughout the property. It crossed the county line into Macon County, damaging more trees and structures in Blue Mound, including the roof of Meridian Elementary School. It also destroyed 2 grain bins south of the school. It tracked east-southeast, taking down electrical transmission lines and numerous large tree branches. It crossed US-51 and tracked east-southeast into Shelby County where it damaged more trees and electrical transmission lines along the Shelby/Macon county line. The tornado lifted 3 miles northeast of Moweaqua along N 1000 East Rd.

A line of thunderstorms with an embedded supercell moved through northeast Blair County the evening of Saturday July 18th. The same storm that produced a tornado about 7 miles to the northwest near Houtzdale produced another tornado along Vanscoyoc Hollow Rd in Camp Anderson. The tornado began just north of Decker Hollow Rd and continued southeastward across Vanscoyoc Run Stream and Camp Anderson Lake before lifting just past the southeast-most campsite. A few trees on the north side of the track fell to the southeast, while several trees on the south side of the track fell northeast or east-northeast, indicating convergence associated with a tornado.

Additional sporadic tree damage was observed farther southeast along Vanscoyoc Hollow Rd, but it was  spread out enough to preclude extension of this tornado path.

We would like to thank the owners of Camp Anderson along with Blair County Emergency Management Agency for their assistance with this survey.
Brief spin-up tornado was observed along the leading edge of a organized bowing segment of thunderstorms.

The tornado began between Glendale Rd and Hartline Rd in the Caywood community, then tracked southeast through the Hills community, knocking over a silo and damaging several homes. The most intense damage and EF2 rating occurred along State Route 26 near the intersection with Township Road 635, where a roughly 600 yard long by 400 yard wide patch of pine trees was completely mowed down with every trunk snapped several feet above the ground. The tornado weakened while still causing sporadic tree damage as it continued to the southeast, crossing the Ohio River on the west side at Newell Run and entering West Virginia at Belmont damaging and rolling several camper trailers at Riverview Estates. The tornado then continued southeast up a ridge then skipped through the Green Run neighborhood before dissipating.

Thanks to the Washington County, OH Sheriff's Office and Emergency Management Agency, who provided excellent video of the track taken by their drone. Also, thanks to Tyler County, WV Search and Rescue for also providing drone imagery and an aerial survey of the track in West Virginia.

The tornado began between Newells Run Rd and Kerr Run Rd, where numerous trees were uprooted and snapped before tracking southeast through Newport, where some minor damage occurred to homes and some sporadic tree damage was noted. The tornado then strengthened as it crossed the Ohio River and entered the West Virginia side at the Saint Marys Bridge. A large sign was left barely hanging off the side of the bridge structure and a large patch of trees around the bridge showed significant damage. From there, the tornado tracked southeast up the hillside reaching peak intensity and a high end EF2 rating near the intersection of Greens Run Rd and Rt 16 where several homes suffered significant damage, a roughly 600 yard wide by 300 yard long patch of hardwood trees was leveled, and a large communications tower was buckled over. The tornado path then became intermittent as it skipped basically along Rt 16 to the Cloverdale community, then ended near the Ritchie County line east of Rock Run Rd. 

Thanks to the Washington County, OH Sheriff's Office and Emergency Management Agency, who provided excellent video of the track taken by their drone. Also, thanks to Tyler County, WV Search and Rescue for also providing drone imagery and an aerial survey of the track in West Virginia.

An EF0 tornado with maximum estimated winds of up to 85 mph began around 5:38 PM just south of Taylors Drain Road along a railroad track. It then traveled southeast along the railroad track before lifting at approximately 5:39 PM. The length of the track is estimated at 0.35 miles, but could be longer given limited road access in the area. Multiple hardwood trees were either uprooted or snapped along the track of the tornado. Some of the hardwood trees that were uprooted were in excess of 18 inches in diameter.

Barbour County now has a total of 5 tornadoes dating back to the late 1800s. The last tornado that occurred in Barbour County was an EF-1 on June 22, 2026 that touched down just northeast of Moatsville, or approximately 6 miles east-northeast of the track of this tornado.

We would like to thank the Barbour County Office of Emergency Management with this damage survey.

The tornado began in the Wayne National Forest near Archers Fork Rd, then tracked southeast through the Leith Community, crossing the Ohio River and entering West Virginia near Raven Rock. The tornado then took a non-continuous path in a southeasterly direction through northern Pleasants County, southern Tyler County, northern Ritchie County, before lifting finally near Arnolds Creek Rd in Doddridge County. 

It is interesting to note that the tornado track became increasingly wide, expanding to three-quarters of a mile wide at the Pleasants/Tyler line, along Rt 74 near Mountain, WV, and along Long Run Rd in Doddridge County, but only EF0 to EF1 tree damage was found in these areas. However, most of the track was over a very rural area with wide spans of forest between the available road network so it is likely that higher end damage was missed by the ground survey.

Thanks to Tyler County, WV Search and Rescue for providing an aerial survey of parts of the track.

The tornado tracked down a hillside, across Leatherbark Rd and then up the adjacent hillside snapping large mature hardwood trees at the center of a nearly half mile wide path. A house near the edge of the track had some shingle damage to the roof. 

Due to the remote location and lack of accessibility, the tornado beginning point and ending points are estimated. The tornado began somewhere between Rt 16 and Leatherbark Rd. The tornado ended somewhere between Lost Ridge Rd and Bean Ridge Rd. 

Thanks to the landowner for access and assistance with this survey.

NWS Damage Survey team confirmed a tornado developed around 11:56 AM CDT just north of Wisconsin Avenue in Appleton with the roof partially torn off several businesses in the area.  The tornado tracked south, intensifying rapidly as it tracked into Winnebago County.  The tornado snapped and uprooted numerous trees and produced damage to several area homes and businesses along its path.  The most significant damage occurred in the Fox Crossing and Menasha areas, where several businesses were heavily damaged near Highway 10 and a house destroyed in Menasha. The heavily damaged areas are consistent with EF-3 tornado damage with estimated winds near 140 mph.

The tornado then continued south over Lake Winnebago, where it dissipated around 12:22 pm CDT.

This tornado appeared to start just east of Interstate 57 and moved eastward, crossing Interstate 80 on the northwest side of Country Club Hills. The tornado then progressed east-northeastward through Hazel Crest, downing trees and tree limbs and removing roofing material off of multiple apartment buildings along 171st Street. After crossing Interstate 80 again at the junction with Interstate 294, the tornado made an unusual counter-clockwise loop as it tracked into the east side of Markham and then the southwest side of Harvey, causing primarily tree and cosmetic structure damage. After reaching its northernmost point between W 154th Street and W 155th Street, the tornado looped back southward, rapidly accelerating as it re-entered Markham and Hazel Crest. The tornado reached its peak intensity here, removing the roof of an industrial building on W 167th Street and causing exterior wall and roof damage to an apartment complex on 171st Street. After crossing Interstate 80 for a third time, the tornado continued southeastward through the north and east sides of Homewood. There, four double-stacked intermodal containers weighing approximately 75 tons each were tipped over in a rail yard, and numerous additional trees were damaged. The tornado caused more tree damage on the northwest side of Glenwood before dissipating near the Glenwood Academy.
Video evidence of a touchdown of a tornado just outside of Hoopeston. Minor damage occurred to two light poles. The tornado traveled to the south for a mile before dissipating behind a bank building.
Public report of a landspout tornado with no known damage.
Approximate track from video evidence of brief touchdown provided by county Emergency Manager.

Ground and drone surveys found a swath of sporadic wind damage from Sweetser to Marion and near Gas City Indiana. Within this swath, evidence of a weak, disorganized circulation touching down was noted in some locations. The tornadic damage began in a cornfield near W 200 N and N 500 W on the north side of Sweetser, IN. The tornado crossed over the cornfield and impacted a neighborhood on the northeast side of Sweetser. Several large tree branches were downed and a few tree trunks snapped on Allen Drive, Mary Lou Road, and Laura Lane. The tornado continued southeast, affecting residences on W Magers Road where significant tree damage occurred including a large tree falling on the roof of a house. Another residence experienced large tree branches downed along with damage to fencing. The tornado crossed N 400 and caused damage to an apartment complex including large tree branches downed and some roof damage to a few of the apartment buildings. The tornado then affected open fields before crossing State Road 18 causing damage to a trucking company facility on the south side of State Road 18. Much of the roofing material was removed, but the plywood boards remained intact. Some of the debris from the damage to this facility was tossed to the north side of State Road 18 including a steel reel. The tornado then continued southeast across open fields between County Roads 325W and 200W before causing extensive tree damage to residences from W 9th Street to W 16th Street between Buffalo Avenue and Norton Avenue. Survey results indicate a transition occurred from tornado damage to straight line wind damage on the south side of Marion to the southeast of State Road 9 and towards Gas City. Maximum winds are estimated around 75 mph.
A very brief touchdown was documented by two independent photos.  The tornado remained in open areas.

An EF1 tornado with maximum estimated winds of up to 95 mph began
around 6:55 PM just west of Whitmer Road midway up Rich Mountain,
or approximately 2 miles northwest of the town of Whitmer. It then 
traveled east-southeast down the steep terrain of the mountain, 
uprooting or snapping numerous trees along its path, with most 
of the damage in the hollow down the side of the mountain.
Some of the hardwood trees that were uprooted were in excess of 18 
to 24 inches in diameter. The tornado continued to the valley at 
the bottom of Rich Mountain, with the last observed damage just 
east of Dry Fork Road. The tornado lifted at approximately 6:57 PM and 
was on the ground for 0.90 miles. 

Randolph County now has 6 documented tornadoes. The last time a 
tornado occurred in the county was 7/9/1980. Two tornadoes 
occurred that day, one was rated an F2, while the other an F1.

This tornado touched down near the intersection of Maple Avenue and Brookbank Road before continuing southeastward through neighborhoods on the south side of Downers Grove. Damage along the path of the tornado consisted of snapped and uprooted trees and downed tree branches. The tornado appeared to lift over McCollum Park. This tornado was within a broader region of straight-line winds and was identified by a corridor of locally more intense wind damage with tree branches torn from the tops of trees as well as a subtle radar debris signature visible on KLOT radar imagery.

Based on a storm survey and radar data from TMDW, a brief EF-0 tornado touched down near or just northeast of the intersection of Illinois Route 53 and Material Services Road across from Romeoville High School. The tornado then traveled southward along Route 53 and passed directly over the campus of Lewis University. Damage on the campus consisted of numerous downed and snapped tree limbs, damage to a dugout and fencing material at a baseball field, and damage to an HVAC system on the roof of a university building. The tornado appeared to lift near Renwick Road.

An EF-0 tornado touched down along Joe Stephens Road. It did some concentrated tree damage in this area. The tornado traveled south/southeast towards Greensburg Road, where it removed part of a roof on the southward face of a mobile home, along with tree damage. The tornado continued southward across the Cumberland Parkway. The most widespread damage was along Columbia Road, where large limbs were toppled on to some homes and some large trees were uprooted. The tornado continued its narrow path through a residence along Breeding Road, where it likely lifted just south of Breeding Road.

A supercell moving across Westmoreland County began showing increasing rotation as the cell moved into northern Somerset County during the early evening hours of Saturday, July 18, 2026. A tornado associated with this supercell formed northwest of Conemaugh Township Reservoir. The damage at tornado onset was mainly in the form of multiple trees being uprooted in a convergent pattern before the tornado strengthened and produced a widespread swath where all trees in the area just west of the reservoir were completely snapped. This entire swath of hardwood trees comprised of mostly healthy hardwood trees with virtually no trees remaining standing in a quarter mile swath. Tree damage continued onto the south end of the reservoir, with multiple snapped and uprooted trees being knocked into the south end of the reservoir before shifting to a more southeasterly path following Ferndale Road for a brief period of time. Concentrated convergent tree damage continued to be observed on Ferndale Drive leading up to the reservoir before the damage became more sporadic and less convergent north of Ferndale Road near Bens Creek. NWS State College would like to thank the Conemaugh Township Municipal Authority for drone imagery of this damage near the reservoir and Somerset County Emergency Management Agency on their collaboration on this damage survey.
This tornado track was identified using satellite imagery and drone overflights.

A brief tornado began near the intersection of Stacy Court and Railroad Street in unincorporated North Glen Ellyn. A narrow corridor of primarily tree damage continued south-southeast across portions of Glen Ellyn. This damage included large branches that fell onto power lines and damaged some homes and a vehicle. Damage in this area was consistent with peak winds near 75 mph. The tornado continued southward, producing additional sporadic tree damage until it dissipated northwest of Glenbard West High School near the intersection of Hawthorne Boulevard and Park Boulevard.

The tornado touched down near W 131st Street near Tampier Slough and moved southeastward across western Orland Park. Numerous trees were downed along the path of the tornado before it lifted in a neighborhood west of Orland Square Mall.

A swath of damaging straight line winds impacted portions of Catawba County on the afternoon of July 28th. This swath of wind damage started along Rifle Range Rd and extended southeast across Lee Cline Rd, NC Hwy 16 and Interstate 40. The intensity of the winds subsided between Interstate 40 and US Hwy 70. Within this swath of damaging winds, many trees were uprooted along with large limbs snapped. The core of the damage occurred along Rifle Range Rd  and Lee Cline Rd near the intersection with Stafford St. Here, peak winds were estimated at 75 mph.

The tornado touched down just east of State Route 394 and progressed northeastward into the community of Lansing. Damage along the path was most severe in a neighborhood near Heritage Middle School where several homes sustained damage to exterior walls and roofs. The tornado continued northeastward, causing primarily tree damage and cosmetic damage to structures while moving into Indiana before lifting on the the far west side of Munster. Two minor injuries were reported in Lansing as a result of this tornado.

An EF-0 tornado, with peak estimated winds of 80 mph, touched down in the Allegheny area of Madison County. Initial tree damage, consisting of broken large branches and a few uprooted or partially snapped trees, was first observed along Rock Branch Road. The tornado tracked southeastward across Highway 212, producing the most concentrated area of damage along the southward-facing slope of Shelton Laurel Creek, where numerous trees were snapped and uprooted. The track continued southeastward to Cutshall Town Road, where several pine trees were snapped. Additional broken branches and possibly a few uprooted trees were noted in a distant wooded area looking back toward the creek. All observed tree damage was consistent with EF-0 intensity.

Although the damage was relatively minor and sporadic, it correlates well with radar data showing a tornadic circulation moving through the area. Due to the rugged, mountainous terrain, earlier portions of the potential track were inaccessible by ground survey teams. The National Weather Service will continue to evaluate the exact start point in the coming weeks if high-resolution satellite imagery becomes available.

A brief tornado occurred in north Pickens County, GA in the late evening hours of July 28, 2026, first producing damage at 10:29 PM EDT. Damage was first observed to the south of the Pickens/Gordon County line, where a few trees were uprooted near a home on Phil Dundee Way. The tornado continued southeast, where it uprooted trees along the northern portion of Outback Rd. To this point, the uprooted trees combined with minimal damage near the ground indicated that the rotation remained mainly elevated, only sporadically touching the surface. As it continued along its southeast path, the tornado brought trees down across E Price Creek Rd and additionally uprooted or snapped trees on Outback Ridge Trail. The most substantial damage occurred near a home at the intersection of Outback Ridge Trail and E Price Creek Rd, where several trees were uprooted and another was snapped. A barrier comprised of 6x6” boards was also pulled from the ground by one tree being uprooted. The elevation of the terrain decreased to the south of this location, though there were signs of disturbance in the trees along the downward slope. The next indicator of damage was observed along Jack Pinyon Rd where a tree was snapped. Additional damage occurred near the intersection of E Price Creek Rd and Mountain Crest Dr where smaller trees and limbs were downed on both sides of the road. After taking a more southerly turn, the tornado last produced damage on Old Burnt Mountain Rd where a partially dead tree was brought down across the road. The tornado appears to have dissipated by 10:33 PM EDT.
A brief tornado moved across a home along German Ave between Hillside Way and Highway 175. Damage was done to multiple trees at the property.

NWS ground survey in addition to high resolution satellite analysis confirmed an EF-0 tornado tracked from northeast of Bayou Gauche to west of Luling, LA in St. Charles Parish. The tornado evident damaged a patch of trees on high resolution satellite imagery and additional damage to marsh vegetation was evident with brief, weak tornado debris signatures also present on KHDC during this time. The tornado continued bending northward in direction as it approached the Blouin Canal with a larger, well-defined tornado debris signature becoming more evident on approach. A large tree was visibly damaged/displaced on high res satellite imagery in addition to other minor tree damage noted near Santa Cruz Ct as the tornado began to weaken and lift. The only minor tree damage was noted by the ground surveyor in the location.

Long-lived funnel cloud associated with a storm southwest of Cedar Rapids resulted in a brief touchdown just north of the Eastern Iowa Airport. This was an EFU tornado, as there is no known damage, with photos and videos indicating a very brief touchdown for less than a minute
Waterspout formed offshore and moved onshore. Waterspout was videoed by several onlookers. Tents were thrown up in the air.

A brief tornado quickly developed and touched down at
approximately 5:20 PM EDT near the corner of Madison Avenue and
Southern Avenue. A large was tree uprooted with a few large
branches and smaller tree limbs scattered around the area.
Additional minor siding damage was done to a nearby home. The
tornado moved north along Madison Avenue causing additional damage
to trees and minor siding damage to another home. A truck trailer
was pushed towards the north denting a parked truck. The tornado
uprooted or snapped a few trees near Christel House South Academy
before quickly dissipating at approximately 5:22 PM EDT.

After review of high resolution satellite imagery and KMOB radar imagery, a new EF0 tornado was found in the Carpenter area. This tornado began along Cliffs Landing Road, tracking east-northeast across D'olive Street before dissipating in the forest. This tornado caused primarily minor tree damage, with a peak width around 100 yards on the south side of D'olive Street adjacent to State Highway 225.

A brief, weak EF0 tornado occurred within a field and adjacent forest between Wiggins Still Road and Mosquito Fork Road. High resolution satellite imagery revealed a narrow, brief path which lined up well with a weak velocity couplet and tornado debris signature identified off KMOB radar data. The tornado caused minor tree damage along its track and was preceded to the northwest by a strong swath of damaging winds estimated in the 70 to 85mph range.

At approximately 6:21 PM, a tornado touched down near Grapevine Road in Bledsoe County and moved northeast into Cumberland County. The tornado uprooted trees, removed shingles, and damaged multiple outdoor buildings and a barn. It continued to track to the northeast crossing a wooded area before lifting near Jerry Edmonds Road.

After review of available high resolution satellite imagery and KMOB radar data it was determined an EF1 tornado occurred primarily within forested areas northeast of Steelwood Lake. Mostly minor tree damage was observed in a narrow, defined path throughout its track. The tornado lifted along Brady Road as the circulation cycled/weakened and a new tornado began to its northeast.

A brief EF1 tornado occurred across the forest adjacent to Hicks Camp Road and the Leaf River in rural southwestern Greene County. This tornado was identified via a combination of high resolution satellite imagery and the presence of a weak radar tornado debris signature visible off of KMOB radar. The tornado caused a narrow path of tree damage, with several trees taken down along Hicks Camp Road. The tornado likely lifted along the Leaf River where any visible tree damage comes to an end.

What likely began as a waterspout moving toward the south-
southwest over the tidal Patapsco River moved onshore along Cox
Creek in the Riviera Beach area of northeastern Anne Arundel
County. A grill was flipped and numerous trees were snapped near
the top, falling in a convergent manner near the intersection of
Waterview Drive and Riverside Drive.

The tornado continued toward the south, where a street sign was
bent and large sections of siding were removed from a house near
the intersection of Waterview Drive and Hilltop Road; numerous
trees were downed in a convergent manner on this block, as well.
Large tree limbs and tree tops were snapped near the intersection
of West End Drive and Park Place, with additional large limbs
twisted off and tops of trees sheared off near the intersection of
West End Drive and Fieldstone Place.

The tornado then crossed Stoney Creek near the bridge on MD-173
Fort Smallwood Road, before felling additional trees and a power
pole prior to dissipating in the Sunset Beach area.

The National Weather Service thanks trained spotters, media, and
local emergency officials for their assistance in this survey.
An EF1 tornado formed along Stoney Point Rd and briefly tracked southeastward, producing sporadic tree damage and minor structural damage before dissipating over Lac Capri.

Drone video from storm chaser shows brief condensation funnel in contact with ground beneath rapidly rotating bowl funnel extending from storm base at this approximate location. Timing is based on chaser's account and radar data.

The start of the weak tornado occurred in Bledsoe County near Grapevine Road about one quarter of mile south of Cumberland County at approximately 621 PM EDT. Several trees were uprooted. No structures were affected in Bledsoe County. This track represents the start and end of the tornado in Bledsoe County. The tornado then continued into Cumberland County before dissipating 4 miles NW of Melvine. The total path length of the tornado was 1.77 miles.
Path noted in Copernicus Sentinel satellite imagery. Damage reported from Grand View Park is in line with path.

A combination of NWS ground surveys and reanalysis of satellite data concluded that an EF-1 tornado with estimated maximum winds of 100 mph occurred east of Whitakerville, which was south of other previously identified tornadoes in the Warsaw area. Satellite data revealed that the tornado began within a forested area between Highway 83 and Highway 65, creating a 150-yard wide scar of uprooted trees. Eyewitness accounts then reported rotation crossing Highway 65 where tree damage became more light and intermittent east of Highway MM. The tornado then damaged roofing of an add-on building of the Warsaw High School where video showed lofting and rotation of the roofing material. After producing damage over 1.6 miles in approximately 2 minutes, the tornado then dissipated around Kindle road where it uprooted trees within a narrow corridor.

The National Weather Service has confirmed an EF0 tornado east of New Lebanon in Montgomery County, Ohio.

The tornado first developed near Germantown Liberty Road, south of Forney Road, where corn field damage and some tree damage were observed. The tornado then moved due north, on a track that closely approximated Snyder Road until reaching US route 35. Along this stretch of Snyder Road, there was extensive tree damage, including a few large trees uprooted or broken near the base. One barn on the east side of Snyder Road lost a portion of its roof.

North of US Route 35, some shingle damage occurred at a business, with a few garage doors damaged at a storage facility. Some additional tree damage was noted to the north of these businesses.

The National Weather Service would like to thank Montgomery County Emergency Management Agency for their coordination.

This brief tornado began in the vicinity of E. Liberty Drive and S. Washington Street south of Wheaton College. A concentrated corridor of damage was noted, particularly in the vicinity of E. Indiana Street and Campbell Avenue and along Pershing Avenue where the tops of several softwood trees were snapped and numerous limbs were downed. Damage in this area was consistent with peak winds near 75 to 80 mph. The tornado continued southward, producing sporadic tree damage until it dissipated in the vicinity of Alchester Drive. 

Additional damage was noted in the area which was likely associated with a swath of damaging straight-line winds that moved through a few minutes after this tornado occurred.

The National Weather Service has updated EF0 tornado during the early
evening of August 1, 2026 in Dearborn and Franklin counties in Indiana.
A concentrated area of damage in southeast Franklin County was updated
to 90 MPH or EF1 damage. 

Damage was first observed just east of Lawrenceville, Indiana along
Batta Road, near the Batta and Legion Road intersection. Some
roof damage to farm buildings was observed, as well as a large farm
wagon overturned. The tornado appeared to cross over farm fields
where crops were flattened. The tornado then crossed Legion Road
where there were several large trees that were damaged or snapped.
Peak wind in this area was estimated to be near 70 MPH.

The tornado continued north-northeast and continued to produce
tree damage as well as garage door damage along Trackville Road just
north of Old Hickory Road. Peak wind in this area was estimated to
be between 70 and 75 MPH.

The tornado continued into southeast Franklin County, where it
strengthened slightly to produce roof damage to a single family home
as well as roof and wall damage to barns. Peak wind in this area
was estimated to be between 75 and 80 MPH.

The tornado continued north-northeast to properties just northwest of
the intersection of Saint Peters and Stone Roads. There was additional
roof damage to a single family home, as well as the destruction of
3 barns, as well as some snapped pine trees and hardwood tree damage.
It was in this area where the peak wind was updated to near 90
MPH or EF1 damage.

The tornado continued to move north-northeast along a narrow path through
southeast Franklin County, producing additional barn and tree damage along
Wewe Hill Road which was consistent with wind damage between 70 and 75 MPH.

The tornado is believed to have dissipated just north of where Wewe Hill
Road becomes West to East, about 2 miles southwest of Cedar Grove.

The National Weather Service would like to thank the emergency
management agencies in Dearborn and Franklin Counties for
their assistance in this damage survey.

Video from local resident shows tornado moving through a wooded area just west of Highway 89. The tornado impacted the resident's farm, causing minor damage to the house and partial roof loss to an outbuilding. Minor tree damage was also noted in the vicinity. Path is based on video footage and details provided by resident.

At approximately 6:22 PM, a tornado touched down near Heiness Road in Fentress County. The tornado snapped treetops and uprooted a few trees. It continued to track to the northeast before lifting near Baseline Road.

The National Weather Service has confirmed an EF0 tornado in Franklin in Warren County, Ohio.

Southwest of Franklin, several large tree limbs were downed along Hamilton-Middletown Road and State Route 73. As the tornado moved northeast, more tree damage was noted on Dayton-Oxford Road, and a segment of a corn field near Water Source Drive was flattened. Just northeast of Water Source Drive, one large metal building at an industrial facility had a large portion of a northwest-facing wall removed, along with a portion of the roof. Damage at this location supported wind speed estimates of 80 MPH, the highest wind speeds from this tornado.

Several tree limbs were downed in a neighborhood near Forest Ave, Chestnut Street, and Park Ave. One house on Park Ave had some siding damage.

The National Weather Service would like to thank the Warren County Emergency Management Agency for their coordination.

The National Weather Service has confirmed an EF1 tornado northwest of Eaton in Preble County, Ohio.

This tornado primarily impacted areas near Surface Road. The first known damage occurred on the 1600-1700 block of Surface Road. There was some minor roof damage to well-built homes. One barn was destroyed, with cinder block wall collapse, and some sheet metal roofing material thrown into the field to the east.

Damage was then observed on the 1300-1400 block of Surface Road, where significant roof damage was noted at two homes, with sections of roofing material entirely removed. This damage supports wind speed estimates of 100 MPH. Other homes in the area had some minor roof damage. Tree damage was also extensive in the back yards of these homes, with several large healthy trees snapped.

Drone images provided by the Preble County Emergency Management Agency also depicted significant corn field damage in the vicinity of Surface Road. This damage also extended well to the east of Surface Road. Some of this corn field damage is from the tornado, but there is also a large expanse of flattened corn to the north of the path of the tornado, especially northeast of the bend on Surface Road. Much of the northern extent of the corn damage is oriented from northeast to southwest, suggesting a wide swath of strong inflow in the opposite direction of the tornado's motion. No damage of any kind was observed closer to State Route 726.

The National Weather Service would like to thank the Preble County Emergency Management Agency for their coordination and assistance.
